speechtext: Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 57, to amend the Oaths of Allegiance Act.
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, on March 13 last the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), the former Minister of Justice, introduced a bill with the same title, "An Act to amend the Oaths of Allegiance Act." Since that bill was introduced and printed further consideration has been given to its terms, with the result that a slightly modified bill has been prepared, which was submitted to the hon. member for Quebec East before its introduction into this house and which has, I think, received his approval. He has already given notice to the house that he is withdrawing the bill introduced by him on 74726-147^
March 13 in order that this bill, which is a modified form of his own, might be considered favourably by the house.
The hon. member for Quebec East, referring to the circumstances under which his own bill was introduced, made a brief reference to the proceedings of the imperial conference of 1926 of which he and the right hon. leader of the opposition were both members. The summary of proceedings of that imperial conference contains the following passage:
The title of His Majesty the King is of special importance and' concern to all parts of His Majesty's dominions. Twice within the last fifty years has the royal title been altered to suit changed conditions and constitutional developments.
The report recites the title of His Majesty which was adopted by royal proclamation in 1901, and then proceeds:
Some time before the conference met it had been recognized that this form of title hardly accorded with the altered state of affairs arising from the establishment of the Irish Free State as a dominion. It had further been ascertained that it would be in accordance with His Majesty's wishes that any recommendation for change should be submitted to him as the result of discussion at the conference.
We are unanimously of opinion that a slight change is desirable, and we recommend that, subject to His Majesty's approval, the necessary legislative action should be taken to secure that His Majesty's title should henceforward read:
"George V. by the Grace of God, of Great Britain, Ireland and the British Dominions beyond the Seas, King, Defender of the Faith, Emperor of India."
On March 12, 1927, the parliament of the United Kingdom, in order to carry into effect the resolution of the imperial conference of 1926, passed the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act, 1927, which appears in the imperial statutes as 17 George V, Chapter 4, Section 1 of this act reads as follows:
It shall be lawful for His Most Gracious Majesty, by his royal proclamation under the Great Seal of the Realm, issued within six months after the passing of this act, to make such alteration in the style and titles at present appertaining to the crown as to His Majesty may seem fit.
Thereafter, on May 13, 1927, a royal proclamation was issued under the Royal and Parliamentary Titles Act providing that His Majesty's style and titles in the English tongue should thereafter be: "George V, by the Grace of God, of Great Britain and Ireland and of the British Dominions beyond the Seas, King, Defender of the Faith, Emperor of India." Since 1927 that style and title has been adopted in Canada and throughout the British dominions in all administrative acts,
231S
Oaths oj Allegiance Act

but the fact that that is not the title prescribed in the Oaths of Allegiance Act of Canada apparently escaped notice until the hon. member for Quebec East brought it to the attention of parliament, and introduced a bill to rectify that anomaly.
At the same time it has appeared expedient that the oath of allegiance in Canada should conform in its terms to the oath of allegiance which was adopted in the United Kingdom in 1868, and which has been adopted in South Africa, Australia and I presume in New Zealand, although I have not had access to the New Zealand statutes. That form of oath is the form suggested to be adopted in the bill now to be introduced.
The anomaly that our oath of allegiance should differ from that which has prevailed in the United Kingdom since 1868 led me to make some interesting researches. I found that the present oath of allegiance presently prescribed in the revised statutes of Canada was adopted by the parliament of Upper Canada on February 13, 1833, by chapter 12 of 3 William IV. In looking into the circumstances \inder which the statute was passed, I find that that was a time of civil strife and turmoil in Upper Canada. Upon the union of Upper and Lower Canada in 1840 the oath which had been adopted in Upper Canada was no longer the oath for the united Canada which came into existence in 1841. The year 1849 was also a time of tumult, civil commotion and excitement and the legislature of old Canada re-enacted in 1850, chapter 18 of 13 and 14 Victoria the form of oath which had been adopted in Upper Canada in 1833.
When the British North America Act was passed in 1867 an oath was prescribed therein in schedule 5 by section 128 of that act. This was a simple form of oath to be taken by senators and members of parliament and did not conform to the somewhat elaborate oath which had been contrived in 1833 in Upper Canada and in 1850 by the legislature of united Canada. The British parliament declined to adopt that form of oath. In 1868 the British parliament 'by special statute, 31-32, Victoria, chapter 72, which came into force on July 31, 1868, a year after the British North America Act, 1867, was enacted prescribed a form of oath to have effect in the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland and throughout the British dominions in so far as the legislation of .the Imperial parliament had force and effect. This simple form of oath prescribed in Great Britain in 1868 is:
I,		, do swear that I will be
faithful and bear true allegiance to Her Majesty Queen Victoria, Her Heirs and successors according to law. So help me God.

There was a provision in this statute that upon the demise of the sovereign, the name of the reigning sovereign of the time should be inserted for .the name of Her Majesty, Queen Victoria. This is the oath of allegiance which is prescribed in the United Kingdom and in all the colonies of the empire and the same form has been adopted in Australia and South Africa. It seems expedient that this dominion should adopt the same form and this is what is proposed in the present bill.
The bill provides for two exceptions. There is a slightly different form of oath to be taken by members of the House of Commons and the Senate, which is prescribed by section 128 of the British North America Act, 1867, and the fifth schedule thereto. We have no authority or at least we do not propose to amend the British North America Act, and therefore we except that act in this proposed legislation. We have excepted also the simple form of oath which is prescribed in our Naturalization Act, which act is similar to .the naturalization act of the United Kingdom. The same form of oath is prescribed in the naturalization acts of South Africa and Australia.
There is one other simple provision. Several statutes of this parliament contain special oaths of office to be taken by special officials. I am informed that when other officials are sworn in, it has been the custom for the clerk of the privy council to improvise such a form of official oath as he deemed expedient under the circumstances. There is in this bill a provision that from time to time the governor in council may prescribe oaths of office, which have not been expressly provided for by parliament, when new offices are created and it becomes necessary to administer oaths of office to the appointees to such offices.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

Mr. Speaker, a question was asked
yesterday by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) based upon a press dispatch that an importation of Swedish pigs was to be made into this country. An answer of yes or no might be misleading and I should like to make a short statement in an endeavour to make clear just what is behind this press dispatch. It is generally recognized that the Danish pig is among the most suitable to produce bacon of the type desired by the consumer in the United Kingdom. This suitability is the result of years of careful selection based on the gain of the pig and the quality of the pig, using feed which is cheapest to feed. That is, the selection is based more on a pig suitable to make use of certain feed rather than the changing of feed and the putting in of considerable research work on feed to make it suitable to any pig. In order to improve the quality of her bacon, Sweden imported some of the best approved herds of Denmark landrace pigs. They carried on the work started in Denmark and the result is that they are now on almost an equal if not an equal footing with the Danish bacon produced by the land-race pigs. For this reason it was felt it would be all gain if there was an importation made into this country from the best of the Swedish herds in order to make a study of their suitability to our country and to our feeds and also with the possibility of crossing with different bacon type hogs used in Canada. Pigs of this type are not available for purchase in the United Kingdom, as referred to in a press dispatch. There was a small importation last fall of white pigs from the United Kingdom. This importation is contemplated, when we receive the assurance of the health of animals departments of the United Kingdom and the United States, that such an importation will not interfere with the understanding between the countries. It is the intention to keep the importation entirely under the control of our government institutions for experimental purposes in order to see how they respond to our conditions, in comparison with our own pigs under similar conditions. If they do not respond, as it is expected they will, they will not be distributed amongst private breeders but will be slaughtered and sold. Every precaution in this connection will be taken if the importation is made.

The house again in committee on Bill No. 40, to amend the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act.-Mr. Weir (Melfort)-Mr. LaVergne in the chair.
On section 2-Exporting agent.
What difficulties have been encountered to necessitate this provision?

In the Live Stock Act authority is given to set a maximum charge which commission men, or people engaging in trade in the stockyards, may make for the handling of stock, and there is also provision that bonds be required for people so engaged in trading in live stock. The act does not cover these

Live Stock and Products Act
particular cases that have come into prominence through our export of cattle, and it was to include exporting agents that these two words were added.
Is this to overcome such a difficulty as was recently encountered in the port of Montreal?
It would be a protection in a case such as that.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-"Public commercial vehicle."
This section will not interfere with the farmer taking his own stock to market?
It simply provides that anyone other than the farmer handling the stock will have to report to the owner the grading and ticket of sale to show what the basis of payment was.

Section agreed to.
On section 4-Regulations.
Will the minister give us a further explanation of this section.

Some of the provinces that desire to improve the quality of their poultry have wished to pass legislation to give them control over the eggs that go into their hatcheries, so that they may be assured they are from approved flocks. That object however cannot be attained; that is to say, they have no control over eggs coming from another province into the territory concerned, and various provinces have asked us to insert this provision in the Live Stock Products Act, so that if they wish to pass enabling legislation they may do so in order to prevent the entry into the province of eggs from flocks that are not approved, and which are intended to be hatched in the hatcheries within the province. If the provinces do not wish to pass legislation, this will not interfere. So far as concerns those that do-and we have had a number of requests- it will enable them to carry out their plans for the improvement of poultry in each particular province.

Has any request come from
British Columbia?
I believe not.
Any request from Quebec?
No.
Any request from Alberta
Yes.
I understand some regulations are at present in force in connection with hatcheries. What are they?
This will not affect them at all.
But there are some regulations in force at present; some supervision is given by federal officials in British Columbia?

Yes. There are
approved hatcheries and approved flocks. The approved flocks are on request approved by federal officials or by provincial officials and the desire is that eggs will not be shipped from one province to another from flocks other than from those approved for use in hatcheries. This provision will not affect any regulation which exists at present in British Columbia in connection with their approved hatcheries.

May I draw to the attention of the minister complaints that have reached me regarding the present regulations in British Columbia, that is, that approval is given to certain hatcheries without investigation as to the source of some of the eggs in the hatcheries, the result being that some men who have approved flocks are at a disadvantage, so to speak, by breeders who have not approved flocks selling to those hatcheries. Difficulty is, I understand, going to arise due to provincial regulations being put into effect in Alberta designed to prohibit importation into that province of day-old chicks unless from approved hatcheries. Those two aspects of the situation should be looked into by the minister and I would like to know whether he has any further information.
No.
At present in British Columbia those regulations are not being enforced, and I believe to the benefit of approved hatcheries.

I would appreciate
it very much if the hon. member would communicate with me and give me specific instances that will enable us to make an investigation of the matter to which he refers.
I shall do so.

I think this clause might
very well be left out. It is dealing with pretty small potatoes, as the expression is,
Live Stock and Products Act

when we interfere in a matter of that kind. The minister has said that the object is to allow regulations which will permit the hatching only of chickens of an approved breed.

No, of approved
flocks. This is very important from the standpoint not only of quality production but especially of disease control.

The suggestion, as he said
a few minutes ago, was that they had been bringing in from another province birds or eggs-
Eggs.
-of an undesirable quality.

From flocks that
were not approved and not certified as free from certain prevalent diseases.

The average man in British
Columbia who raises chickens, makes a hobby of it and wants to increase the quality of his flock, will hardly go to the expense of bringing in inferior eggs from another province. It would not be sensible to do so. He will naturally bring in eggs from an approved breeder or approved hatchery or someone who has a reputation. He would not bring in inferior eggs from a distance because that would make them very expensive. If he wanted inferior eggs, he could get them next door.

This applies only
to commercial hatcheries, but I know from personal experience there are commercial hatcheries that advertise under more or less fictitious certificates. The certificate is a very fine looking document so long as one does not investigate it, and yet there may be no registration behind the birds, no selection made and no guarantee that they are from approved flocks or flocks disease-free. This provision will not interfere with the small chicken farmer; it will affect only commercial hatcheries as a protection against disease and inferior birds.

On section 7-Failure to comply with requirements.

Does this mean that an ordinary buyer of cattle at a point of assembly shall be required, in order to comply with this provision, to fill in special forms issued by the government?
(Mr. Neill.]

No, it has nothing whatever to do with that. In the Live Stock Act power is given to the Department of Agriculture to set a maximum charge to be made by live stock commission firms in the handling of live stock. If it is felt that the charge is too high, notice is given that it should be reduced, but previously the period of time between the notice being given and the ministerial order being issued and put into effect was sixty days. I would

At first sight it might be felt that this was taking away some of the protection from the farmer selling his stock. May it not be implied that the government is accepting the responsibility for the administration of the trust account?

Yet as the minister is providing the regulations for the administration of and payments from the account does it not appear possible that there arises some responsibility?

It is claimed that this clause in our Live Stock Act cannot be

Canada Grain Act

I am
wondering if the minister may not be stepping into a possible difficulty. There is no doubt whatever that he is now cancelling a provision of the old act with respect to the obligation of the bank concerning trust accounts and is himself going to provide the regulations. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that yesterday, in the discussion of this very important measure, I made it very clear-and I suppose this applies to most hon. members on this side of the house-that as far as I am concerned I agree with many features and the spirit of the bill. We realize that the old policy of laissez faire is a thing of the past, and that to-day we must have to some extent a system of planned economy. Of course, in dealing with a matter of this kind we may go to extremes. We reached an extreme under the old policy and to-day, in order to maintain an even keel in the national life of this country, we must be careful that we do not go to the other extreme.
We must not expect the government to take over all our social and most of our personal activities. This bill implies the interference of the government in many of the activities of our daily lives, and that is why I have been opposing som# of the features which it contains. We must remember, of course, that we cannot continue indefinitely to enlarge and implement further the policies of the past. We have seen many changes take place. In connection with our external trade, for instance, in the last twenty-five or thirty years we have made treaties with other nations of the world, while before that time the matter of external trade was left largely to corporations and individuals. We have seen the curtailment of our wheat acreage, which was agreed to by the right hon. Prime Minister after the conference last summer. This was another step in the direction of governmental regulation if not absolute governmental control. I feel that one of the main reasons for this act is to secure the sanction of parliament to the curtailment of our wheat acreage in the western provinces in order to have uniformity of policy in that direction. So I believe we have been courting government control for the last dozen years at least, and no one can say that I personally or the Liberal party are opposed to some of the principles contained in the bill now before the house, and the enlargement of that principle. I stated yesterday, Mr. Speaker, that doubtless the capitalistic system has sinned, but at least it has shown that it can supply all the requirements of the people. The situation we have to face to-day, however, is not so much a question of production and regulation as it is a ques-

tion of distribution and of the purchasing power of the people. Notwithstanding anything that people may say to the contrary and notwithstanding what appears in this bill, the consumer must be primarily concerned with this measure.
There are other causes as well which have contributed indirectly to the present situation, and which have brought about the legislation now before us. One very important contributing cause of the depression was the financial structure of many of our corporations, the watering of stocks, the terrible gambling which we witnessed for six or seven years, and so on. A series of articles appeared in the Montreal Daily Herald during the course of last winter which indicated very plainly that the people of this country have been mulcted to the tune of nearly four billion dollars. In nickel stocks alone, for example, the Canadian people have lost at least $900,000,000. I am not going to read any of these articles since I believe they were distributed to all hon. members of this house and of the Senate, but I should like to refer to some of the headlines that appeared in connection with that series of articles:

Not only the big corporations with nationally known names, but thousands, if not tens of thousands, of the smaller corporations found it possible under the existing government regulations to squeeze the people to the tune of some four billions of dollars. That has been one of the main causes of the depth of this depression. We had the spectacle of European peoples sending across their gold and their money to carry on gambling in the New York market in a way that had never been done before during those so-called prosperous years. The government must be seized of these facts and should find a way of dealing with them. I know that the committee on mass buying intends to deal with the matter, but it is of such great importance that it is imperative that action be taken at once if we want to bring back prosperity to this country.
Some hon. members may think that it was only the so-called big fellow who was in the market, but this orgy of gambling reached throughout the rank and file of our Canadian people. On many occasions I myself have seen in the town of Timmins, for example, the miners coming from their work, still carrying their dinner pails, sitting before the stock boards to watch the quotations. I have seen people in all walks of life throwing more and more of their savings into this form of gambling, because it is gambling pure and simple, and the worst possible kind of gambling, for in a poker game there may be some chance, but it has been well proven by the Montreal Herald that in the stock market the dice are loaded against the smaller speculator, the little fellow, who had no chance of winning from the start.
I want to be fair, Mr. Speaker. I know that the government is sincere in wanting to go to the root of our present social evils, but I repeat that this has been the greatest cause of the depression that we are now experiencing, for the savings of our people were turned away from proper commercial and industrial channels and thrown into the stock market.
The bill that is now before us is leading to government control with a vengeance. As I stated a few moments ago, there must be some measure of control applied, as it has been applied in the past, and it is probable that the measure of control will have to be enlarged to some extent.
Let me review briefly what absolute government control has led to in other countries. Will anyone say, for instance, that absolute government control in soviet Russia, control of all the activities of that great population,
has been beneficial to the working men and the farmers? Hon. gentlemen no doubt remember the statement that was made by the hon. member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mitchell), who is very impartial in his views and fair-minded in his utterances. He told us after his visit to Russia last year that the situation he found there was most deplorable, that it could hardly be conceived.
Is Italy in a better position than she was a few years ago? Italy has an absolute dictatorship, absolute government control of all the social and commercial and industrial activities of that great nation. You can always judge a tree by its fruits. Only a few days ago the prime minister of Italy asked the Italian people to tighten their belts a little more, and that after having had full control of all the activities of that great nation for a number of years, with the people of the nation working together almost as a solid unit. After years of application of the government policy of absolute control, the prime minister of Italy tells the people that they must tighten their belts a little more. The belts of Canadian people are not as slack perhaps as wTe would like them to be, but I would like to see any prime minister in this country or any leader of any great party go before the Canadian electors and tell them that they must tighten their belts a little more. I believe that shows, Mr. Speaker, that absolute government control would not be applicable to this country.
It is true that the capitalistic system has sinned very grievously, but I believe that there are honest and sincere men in the higher positions in our industrial and financial life, and I believe that much can be done by cooperation and coordination between our industrial leaders and all other activities, and the government to solve many of our difficulties at the present time.
We cannot get away from the fact that this marketing bill now before us is intended to give a greater measure of control over the activities of our primary producers. It is true that the farmers were the first class of our population to suffer in the depression. Why? For one very good reason, and that was that they were not organized to curtail production. Mind you, I am not in favour of working against the designs of Providence. Regardless of what other people may say, I have faith in Providence, and when I am told that nations, and indeed whole continents, are planning to curtail production I have some fears, I nevertheless believe that there is a better solution of our problems. But the farmers were unable to get or maintain

Marketing Act-Mr. Bradette
higher prices for their production because of the lack of organization amongst them, and then they found themselves with over-production. That was not because of more bountiful crops, but when unemployment came in the cities and men were thrown out of work, when labour became cheaper for it is simply a question of supply and demand and when labour is plentiful wages go down, the urban population lost almost fifty per cent of its buying power within a year. The results of that were felt more severely by the agricultural class in this country than any other.
To-day an attempt is being made in this country to curtail the acreage of wheat, and indeed the bill before us, if I understand it aright, is based on the principle of curtailing production or at all events maintaining artificial prices. I never have believed in artificiality, whether applied to industry or any other class of the community. I believe in the natural course of nature, which can be helped to a certain extent only by legislation and governmental regulation. Surely in this country we are not going to try to make our Canadian people as alike as two peas. Have we not confidence enough in their individualism to allow them to work out their own destinies, and abstain from interfering unless some form of regulation is absolutely demanded? Are we going to say that no one shall be allowed to glow a bushel of wheat or catch a pound of fish or produce goods of any kind without the dictation of government officials? I certainly give the government credit for all the intelligence and administrative capacity it possesses, but no one can make me believe that the primary function of government is not legislative and administrative. The course of history shows us that after the different units of population became large enough, governments were formed for the greater convenience of society, and that applies to Canada. But governments do not possess creative power. That belongs to the individual. Take the evolution of industry and the development of new inventions, for instance. Who will dare to say that these inventions are due to the inventiveness of the government? The suggestion would be absurd because that is not the role of government. The government role is to legislate in such a way that its legislation will be beneficial to all sections of the population.
So far as this bill is concerned, I fully appreciate that there are certain principles that must be followed and accepted, and those principles are not new because they have been

practised in this country for a number of years. There must be some regulation but there certainly should be no regulation in an autocratic manner. I have not the time at the present moment to go into the details of this bill. I believe hon. members should take the opportunity both on second reading and in committee to discuss every phase of it. I am discussing this all-important problem from the viewpoint of the people whom I represent at the present moment. I represent a constituency which is partly industrial, partly mining and partly rural. There are located in my constituency some of the largest gold mines on the North American continent; we have some of the finest rural sections in Canada part of the Northern Ontario clay belt, and we have also great industrial centres like Kapuskasing, Iroquois Falls and Smooth Rock Falls. I have received hundreds of letters from people in my constituency, some for and some against this bill. They all ask that there should be a thorough discussion. The people in my constituency are very sincere and they appreciate the problems which we have to face at the present moment. Although they did not all have an opportunity of reading the bill, some are absolutely in favour of it while others are absolutely against it. The principle which applies to my riding applies also to the government. The government should be careful and not swing too much in one way or the other, they should endeavour to keep an even keel. Some of the people who have written me appreciate the need of a certain amount of governmental regulation but in most cases they contend that this regulation should not take away the initiative of the individual^
In most parts of this country we are still in the pioneering stage. I cannot visualize the time when the government will be the mother, the father, the director and the leader of all our actions, whether personal, industrial or otherwise. Some latitude should be given to the intelligence, the integrity and the activity of our people which has been so well displayed in the past. I can speak as a farmer and I can speak also as a common labourer because as a young man I earned my bread by the sweat of my brow. I would be quite willing to go back again to manual labour. I know the aspirations of the people and I know what the men in the shanties and working manually are thinking. Twenty or thirty years ago I spent my winters in the shanties, but in those days the government did not mean so much to the Canadian people. To-day we expect the government to give us everything. The government has a certain duty to perform in an administrative and legislative way hut

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
I repeat that they have no right to interfere with the personal actions of the people. The government have no right to dictate to the people and say what they shall do to-day or to-morrow, but they have the right to control certain of their activities. I have faith and confidence in our Canadian people. I believe in the spirit which is so well expressed in every section of the British Empire, the spirit of initiative and individualism, the spirit of respect for authority and concern for the welfare of our national life. We do not need drastic measures whereby our every step will be checked.
I mentioned yesterday the difference which exists between this bill and the English act and I pointed out that the principles which apply here are not the same as those which apply in Great Britain. This government intends to regulate certain provincial activities. We are quite ready to-day to blame the newsprint industry for their orgy of building mills and causing over-production; we contend that they should have known that the newsprint market, particularly that of the United States, was being well taken care of and even was saturated; but a few years ago we could not have visualized a federal marketing board which would have dictated to the Honourable Mr. Ferguson or the Honourable Mr. Taschereau their line of conduct at a time when they were asking the financiers of this country to invest their money in newsprint mills in northern Ontario or Quebec. The provincial premiers at that time would not have tolerated any interference from the central government because they maintained, and perhaps rightly so, that they were better acquainted with the situation. No one would have dared to criticize Mr. Ferguson when he was trying to induce American capital to come into northern Ontario and invest in timber limits, water power and newsprint plants, and the same thing applies to Mr. Taschereau of Quebec. Who would have dared to dictate to the Manitoba government in connection with their power developments? Can anyone contend that this marketing bill will foresee all the activities of the future, whether social, industrial or otherwise? Will anyone contend that he can foretell what will happen five or ten years from now? In 1927, 1928 and 1929 there was an apparent shortage of power in Ontario and who could have foretold at that time that in 1934 we would have a surplus?
I believe in the cooperative spirit of the people and we must fully realize the situation we are facing. I should like to mention
I believe this act has been misnamed, it should be the national regulatory act. Codes have been established in the United States but I do not see anything of that kind in this bill, giving no protection to the small farmers, labourers and consumers.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subtopic: ORGANIZATION TO IMPROVE METHODS AND PRACTICES IN MARKETING NATURAL PRODUCTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. member for North Timis-kaming (Mr. Bradette) for admitting so frankly that the capitalist system is not one hundred per cent perfect. I think a further study on his part will reveal to him that the evils which he notes, especially those which were recorded in the article from the Herald from which he read, are inherent in the system.
From my point of view this measure is one of the most significant ever introduced in this house. It may or it may not accomplish the good or, on the other hand, the evil anticipated but it is remarkable in its tendencies. Many of its provisions are vague but I assume that in the discussion in committee their meaning will be fully ascertained. There are certain essential safeguards which seem to be entirely lacking and the operation of the bill is so dependent upon concurrent or enabling provincial legislation that it is next to impossible at this stage to forecast the actual working out of the proposals. However, I would say that the underlying principles are fairly clearly defined. Instead of there being only one principle involved, it seems to me .that there are two principles involved in this bill. First, there is the government control of the marketing of certain natural products and derivatives thereof and, second, the bill affords another example of what is coming to be known as administrative legislation, that is, the granting to the government of certain general powers which it may carry out by means of regulations.
I should like to point out that this measure involves farreaching political consequences. It may very well mean much more than what appears on the surface, it may possibly involve the realignment of the political parties and organizations in Canada. I take it that by introducing this legislation the Conservative party is definitely committed to extending government control over industry; I can read the bill in no other light. Indeed, if the C.CF. had introduced legislation of this kind I can fancy there would be hurled at us the charge that it was socialistic, communistic, bolshevistic and all the rest of it, and that
2328	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
we were destroying initiative and were all going to be regimented. The hon. member for Timiskaming has already suggested that in his speech.
Surely this is a great change in practice for the Conservative party. In this connection I recall an editorial which I read in the Ottawa Journal of May 3, 1929, entitled "Too Much Paternalism." This, I may observe, was in regard to certain insurance legislation. The editorial in question read:
It is to be hoped that parliament and the government find a resting place for these recommendations in the most convenient waste basket. And the reason is clear. It is that if Canada keeps heeding all the reports that are made by committees, and goes on doing all the things that a lot of well-intentioned but misinformed people want her to do, then this country will become so burdened with paternalism and bureaucracy that the taxpayer will be crushed into the earth. Already, indeed, the hand of the state is everywhere. Yet, not satisfied with this, and despite complaints against the ever-increasing cost of government, we have men advocating insurance against unemployment.
It is absolute nonsense. This country has no more need' of unemployment insurance than it lias need of polygamy. In a country like England, over-populated, and where industrial and economic conditions are entirely different from our own, there is something to be said for it. But in Canada, sparsely settled, lacking in population, and passing through an era of tremendous development, the proposition that it is necessary to insure our people against unemployment is absurd. Its only result would be to add to the cost of government, to produce more bureaucrats, and to discourage what is a real insurance against unemployment in Canada, namely, thrift and industry. . . ,
During the past few years we have seen Canada go in for a lot of expensive frills which, when first proposed, were widely ridiculed. And the reason is that any organized minority, if it wants to make enough noise, can put over most anything upon an indifferent and lethargic majority. That is why we are going further and further toward paternalism, looking more and more to the state to do things for us, and getting away from the old wholesome practice of individual effort.
Well, this measure says goodbye to all that. I do not think I need deal with the question of the liberty of the subject; it was very well dealt with by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling). I confess that some of us who were brought up more or less in the general principles of economy as taught by the Manchester school have had some little difficulty in adjusting our thinking to the new world situation. For example when some years ago it was proposed to have a 100 per cent wheat pool I myself found it very difficult to acquiesce in the proposal. And yet, when one studies the situation, such proposals are after all only an extension of certain practices with which we have become familiar.

In my own city some years ago we desired to have a new water works system. A vote was taken and the majority of the people were in favour of the system, so that we put through the necessary legislation and installed the water works. Previously a man might have sunk a well in his backyard. He might as an individual have been opposed to the new arrangement, but under our municipal practice as sanctioned by the people, a bill was put through the legislature. The majority of the people felt that they ought to have a pure water supply and the minority had to come to terms and participate whether they wished it or not.
I have wondered, however, whether the government is prepared to carry out some of the implications of this principle under which the minority rights must be set aside in the interests of the general welfare. I hope the Prime Minister will not think I am taking advantage of his very generous hospitality to-day when I say that this train of thought was suggested by the speech of the Postmaster General of Australia. I find that in Australia when the majority of the bondholders were willing to accept a lower rate of interest the minority of the bondholders were, in his very happy phrase, "asked to agree." I would suggest that if the principle underlying this legislation is adopted by the government and the house as a whole we may as a next step hope for a referendum of bondholders with a view to reducing the rate of interest, and in that case the minority would be asked to agree. Of course, there would be nothing in the way of their being dragooned!

speechtext: Does my hon. friend find that in the bill?

speechtext:
No, but the principle of the bill might be extended into other spheres. Perhaps I would not be going too far if I congratulated the Conservative party on its virtual acceptance of some of the C.C.F. policies. Undoubtedly the British Marketing Act had a great influence in the drafting of this bill, and that act was originally drafted you will recall by a Socialist Labour minister in Great Britain. It is quite true that the act was subsequently modified before being adopted by the present British government, but it owes a great deal to its original drafting, and the original legislation was introduced as part of a definite and general scheme.
The trouble is that the present legislation might be described as patchy or streaky. It is a bit of socialism introduced into the capitalist system, and possibly -we should re-

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworlh
member the scriptural admonition against the sewing of a new patch on an old garment. If that is attempted the very great danger is that the rent will be made worse. I am afraid that this patchy legislation will not cure some of the major evils from which we are suffering at the present time.
While I congratulate the Conservatives on introducing this legislation even though I have tried to point out some of its weaknesses, and while I am a bit dubious whether or not the government will enact other legislation in harmony with it, I would say that the Liberals, by this bill, are placed in a very bad predicament. The leader of the opposition, quite honestly I think, still clings to the old laissez faire school of thought. He is heartily backed, of course, on every occasion by our friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young), and I am looking forward to that hon. gentleman's denunciations. We have already heard from the members for Last Mountain, Hants-Kings, West Edmonton, and others. They have already decided to oppose the bill on the ground, very largely, that it is an unwarrantable extension of governmental authority and an interference with the rights of the subject. I suppose they will have behind them, generally speaking, the Liberal sentiment of the present government of Quebec. On the other hand, may I point out that their position is weakened somewhat by the fact that the president of the National Liberal Federation has already departed very substantially from that attitude. At an earlier stage in the session I called attention to the speech delivered by Mr. Massey at Lake Couchiching on The New Economic Nationalism and I quote again for I think this is rather significant:
It's a difficult world to live in; we are *witnessing the very transition between old laissez-faire improvising ways of doing things, and a tightly planned modern state system. We have to plan our own recovery in this easy-going country of ours, our own reconstruction, our own relationship to this new world.
And again:
The primary conflict is not therefore isolation versus internationalism but planning versus improvisation, and in this trouble planning will,
I believe, be victorious.
Once again:
It must suffice for me to say that national planning will have to be the foundation of Canada's international relations. Old conceptions of government must give place to new.
As I said before, I heartily agree with Mr. Massey's statement. Further than that, even such a sturdy organ of Liberalism as the Free Press of my own city is driven, in special
cases, to abandon its old position. I notice an editorial in it of some months ago, July 31, on More Milk Regulation as follows:
The whole argument for milk regulation is based on the vital importance of that commodity to the community. Any alert, intelligent public health policy must seek to assure all classes of the people of an adequate supply of milk of good quality. For the healthy growth of children this is particularly important. The effect of a better-than-usual supply of milk for the children of families on relief has been noted by many. It is necessary, therefore, that the retail price of milk should be kept as low as possible, and that requires that the spread between the price to the producer and that to the consumer should be no more than is reasonably necessary. That can only be assured if the distribution is on an efficient economic basis.
The most striking thing revealed by a consideration of the present distribution system is that it is anything but economic. It is extremely wasteful and inefficient. The competition has led to the establishment of more plants for the pasteurization and handling of the milk than are necessary and many more wagons than would be required if the companies were not following one another around in all parts of the city. This wasteful duplication is paid for by the consumers, including many who can ill-afford it.
That is precisely the situation which has developed in our city and I believe it is situations of that kind which the bill before us is designed to meet. Moreover, the Liberals are having their difficulties because of the defection of large numbers of younger Liberals throughout the country who, perhaps, are more flexible in thinking and realizing the need of a change in policy. The outstanding example now is that of British Columbia where Mr. Pattullo has come out with certain legislation that is remarkably similar to the bill we are at present discussing and which is an entire abandonment of the old laissez-faire policy. I understand that the only possible way in which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) can answer those who appeal to him against Mr. Pattullo is by bringing forward another Liberal principle that he does not believe the dominion should enter upon a discussion of provincial matters; that each province should be autonomous. That may do for the time being, but it does not alter the fact that Liberals all over are being forced out of their old position.
In this matter the government it seems to me, is in rather a happy position because it has the support at least of the governments of the west. British Columbia, a Liberal government; Alberta, a U. F. A. government; Saskatchewan, a Conservative government and Manitoba, a Bracken-Liberal government-
2330	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
all these are more or less committed to the principle underlying this bill. So far as laissez-faire is concerned, the stars in their courses are surely fighting against Sisera. I think I cannot but take advantage of this opportunity to place before the house the position of our own organization in this matter of external trade. Plank No. 5 reads:
The regulation in accordance with the national plan of external trade through import and export boards-
Canada is dependent on external sources of supply for many of her essential requirements of raw materials and manufactured products. These she can obtain only by large exports of the goods she is best fitted to produce. The strangling of our export trade by insane protectionist policies must be brought to an end. But the old controversies between free traders and protectionists are now largely obsolete. In a world of nationally organized economies Canada must organize the buying and selling of her main imports and exports under public boards and take steps to regulate the flow of less important commodities by a system of licences. By so doing she will be enabled to make the best trade agreements possible with foreign countries, put a stop to the exploitation of both primary producer and ultimate consumer, make possible the coordination of internal processing, transportation and marketing of farm products, and facilitate the establishment of stable prices for such export commodities.
Permit me to say that the government in this bill goes much further in the direction of bureauracy than we in the C. C. F. would like to see, because we believe that whilst there must be some sort of social control, we should do our utmost to avoid centralized control and on the other hand rather encourage the development of cooperative institutions. The lack of such provision in this bill is one of its most serious deficiencies. In this connection may I read our plank No. 6 on cooperative institutions.
The encouragement by the public authority of both producers' and consumers' cooperative institutions-	'
In agriculture, as already mentioned, the primary producer can receive a larger net revenue through cooperative organization of purchases and marketing. Similarly in retail distribution of staple commodities such as milk, there is room for development both of public municipal operation and of consumers' cooperatives, and such cooperative organization can be extended into wholesale distribution and into manufacturing. Cooperative enterprises should be assisted by the state through appropriate legislation and through the provision of adequate credit facilities.
In this particular bill it would seem as if the state itself undertakes not merely the supervision but the actual administration of the marketing of goods. We on our part would rather see a larger measure of local cooperation.

I said that the bill contained very far-reaching provisions with regard to regulated products. Clause 4 indicates this. I do not think I need read it in detail, but it gives the board power:
To regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product-
And so forth.
To exempt from any determination or order any person or class of persons-
And so forth.
To compensate any person for loss sustained-
And so on. Clause 9 is also decidedly far-reaching as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) stated yesterday. I should like to ask: Why limit the control to natural products and to food or drink derived therefrom? Why not have control over manufactured products? If the breakfast foods would come under this legislation, and I think they would according to the terms of the clauses, why not clothes? If drink, we will say beer, would come under the terms of this legislation, why not furniture? It is all very well for the minister to tell us that all he contemplates is agricultural products, but the terms of the bill go much further than that. It would seem to me that the revelations coming out in connection with the price spreads committee clearly indicate that in connection with the processing we have great evils, and that we should exercise some sort of control not merely in the marketing of our natural products but also in the processing of them. Further than that, we should not limit its scope merely to food and drink derived from this class of natural products. Just how far the principle might carry us is indicated by the emergency action of the British cabinet back in 1921. I hold in my hand an article from the Manchester Guardian of April, 1921. Under that emergency action such provisions were included as:
That it shall be lawful for the Minister of Transport, the Board of Trade, and any other department approved for the purpose, and any person duly authorized by a department on whom powers are conferred by this regulation, where it appears necessary to do so, to take possession of any land, buildings or works (including works for the supply of gas. electricity, or water, and of any sources of water supply) and any property (including plant, machinery, equipment, and stores) used or intended to be used in connection therewith.
The Minister of Transport and the Commissioners of Works are empowered to take possession of any land, buildings, or other property for the purpose of providing accommodation in connection with any scheme of

Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
road transport or for housing persons engaged thereon, or of feeding or supplying necessaries to such persons.
The Admiralty, Army Council, Air Council, Minister of Transport, Commissioners of Works, and any other department approved for the purpose, are empowered to take possession of any food, forage, material, or stores, and any articles required for or in connection with the production thereof. After such department has issued a notice of possession any person who sells, removes, or secretes such material without consent, or deals contrary to conditions that may have been granted will be guilty of an offence against the regulations.
I mention this merely to show what would be involved if the principle contained in this bill were applied to other departments of our life.
Now there are several questions which I should like to ask the minister and the house. Three questions are outstanding in my mind as I read this bill. The first is, will the act benefit the producers unless there is a guaranteed minimum price? It seems to me that this is one of the fundamental questions involved in the present wheat situation. I cannot see that any government is justified in forcing the farmers to reduce the export of wheat, which means in practice more or less to reduce their acreage, unless there is supplementary legislation which provides that the farmers will be able to maintain a decent standard of living. Surely complementary to regulation, price fixing legislation is inevitable. That question I should like to have answered very definitely by the minister at some stage in this discussion.
The second question that occurs to me is, What provision is there for the protection of the consumer? In the British procedure more or less protection for the consumer is provided in the set up of the scheme. There are at least two committees, and provision for consumers' investigation. The publicity that is provided for, under I think section 9 of the British act, is to a considerable extent a safeguard to the public; yet notwithstanding these safeguards we find in practice that consumers are complaining a great deal about the actual working out of the British act. In the bill now before us I can find no protection whatever for the consumer.
The third question is, What about the employees? Personally I am strongly in favour of protection to the farmer, but if you protect the farmer you must surely protect his hired man. There must be some protection for farm labour. But nothing of that kind is included in the bill. Then again while certain secondary products come under this act, that is, food or drink wholly or partly manufactured or derived from any such product, it is not at all clear that those em-74726-148
ployees engaged in the processing are to have any protection. It is fresh in our minds that only a few months ago there was a strike in Stratford in connection with the packing plants. The employees were urging that they should receive an advance from 2 cents to 3 cents for each bird plucked. It would seem to the ordinary man that that was not an unreasonable demand, but it was denied by the packing companies. There ought to be very definite provision in legislation of this kind that the employees in any processing industry should be adequately protected. We have further illustrations in the revelations that are coming to us through the so-called Stevens committee. There is no doubt whatever that many employees are being paid much less than a living wage. In this legislation we are apparently overcoming some of the difficulties that have arisen through the division of jurisdiction as between the dominion and the provincial, so it would seem that we might incorporate into this act some sort of minimum wage legislation for those engaged in the manufacture of articles derived from natural products.
As there are a great many details and technical questions to be considered in relation to this bill, the proper procedure would be to send it to the agriculture committee where the experts might be heard. I cannot see how in any other way we can discuss the details with any very beneficial result.
There are several other matters to which I should like briefly to call attention in the time at my disposal. I would note that the central bank is being placed by the government under independent control. Why then, should this marketing board be in the direct control of the minister? That seems to me a great inconsistency. I should think that all the arguments which the government brought forward for the creation of an independent board to handle the money of this country would apply equally to the handling of agricultural products of this country. Further I note that in the setting up of a marketing scheme normally there is to be a petition from a representative number of the producers. There is no indication as to what constitutes a representative number. In the British act that is provided for. It seems to me that this is very loose indeed. Further there is no indication as to who is to bear the cost of such a petition. In the British act there is an arrangement under which the whole cost does not rest upon the producers. Especially in this country, where we are 60 widely scattered, I can understand that the bill as it now stands might work a very great hardship upon the cooperative organizations.

2332	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Woodsworth
With regard to the section dealing with compensation, I am informed that in the Argentine the government has a monopoly of exchange and charges the importers in order to compensate the exporters. If our producers are to be compensated because of an adverse exchange it seems to me that we might very well charge the importers, who are benefiting by that self same adverse exchange. If we had some sort of clearing house in which arrangements of that kind could be made it would seem to me to be desirable.
We are told that we have before us a very important constitutional question. We have had difficulty because of the British North America Act, and I am told that although the provinces cannot delegate their authority to the dominion and the dominion cannot delegate its authority to the provinces, by the device of this marketing board in some mysterious way both can delegate authority, and it is presumed that this covers the whole ground. Hence it is said that the marketing board may have authority which can be secured neither by the provinces nor by the dominion. I am not a constitutional lawyer but I should like very much to have that point cleared up. In the meantime may I point out that under section 95 of the British North America it would seem that in any case the dominion government has very wide powers with regard to marketing. Section 95 reads:
In each province the legislature may make laws in relation to agriculture in the province, and to immigration into the province; and it is hereby declared that" the parliament of Canada may from time to time make laws in relation to agriculture in any or all of the provinces, and to immigration into any or all of the provinces;
This is what I should like noted:
-and any law of the legislature of a province relative to agriculture or to immigration shall have effect in and for the province as long and as far only as it is not repugnant to any act of the parliament of Canada.
So it would seem to a layman at least that we need not worry too much with regard to the difficulty of jurisdiction if this dominion parliament acts in the matter.
I said a little while ago that the great difficulty I found in the proposed legislation was that it was simply one particular act, an attempt to bring about governmental regulation in one department of our public life. I ventured to say that was something like sewing a new piece of cloth on an old garment. In some way we must work out a new system. Mr. Speaker, on the second reading of a bill the first important consideration is that of distinguishing between the purpose of the bill and the principle which underlies its provisions. The purposes of the bill are usually set forth in the name given the measure itself, and the provisions of the bill indicate by their wording the principles upon which they are based. With respect to the measure now before the house the purpose is adequately described in the title, which reads:
An act to improve the methods and practices of marketing of natural products in Canada and in export trade, and to make further provision in connection therewith.

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
As to the desirability of a purpose to be served, as thus expressed, I think all parties in this house will be in entire agreement. There is need for improved methods and practices in the marketing of natural products; there can be no doubt of that, and there is also need for improvement in methods of furthering export trade. Those are highly commendable objects, and any provisions which will further those ends without injury to production and trade of the country or depriving individuals of rights, liberties and privileges which are sacred to all will, I believe, at this time, receive general endorsation. When, however, we come to discuss the question of the principles underlying this measure, we find that the means taken to effect these very desirable ends are questionable indeed and it is in these provisions that the principles are to be found on which the bill itself is based.
May I pause for a moment to say to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), who has just taken his seat, that when he says the Liberal party is a party of laissez-faire he entirely misrepresents its position.

The Liberal party at no time has been a party of laissez-faire. If one takes the history of Liberalism, either in the old land or in this land, one will find that most of the statutes relating to compulsory education, to industrial and social legislation, legislation respecting the regulation of factories, mines, shops and the like, and in this parliament, legislation respecting fair wages in government contracts, investigation of industrial disputes, combines, old age pensions and the like have been enacted at the instance of the Liberal party, and all these enactments have been in the nature of regulation and control. The Liberal party stands for regulation and control, but it stands for such regulation and control at the instance of parliament and not at the instance of bodies that are in no way responsible to parliament or to the electors of the country, and therefore without the necessary authority in the making of the laws.
The supreme consideration at the moment, it seems to me, is not whether we are to have regulated trade or regulated marketing -it is generally agreed that regulation is necessary-but whether that regulation is to be carried on by bodies which, under our constitution, are expected to legislate in matters of the kind or by powers delegated to special interests, or groups, or individuals with no responsibility to parliament or the people as 74726-148 i
a whole; in other words, whether parliament is to continue to be responsible for legislation as we have been for the most part up to to-day, or whether we in parliament are to divest ourselves of this obligation and transfer it to some bodies that hitherto have not had authority to effect those ends. That is a very large question, and it goes to the very heart of the situation in the world today. I know that in many parts of the world at the present time there is a tendency to get rid altogether of parliamentary institutions. In some countries the effort to get rid of them has taken the form of turning over government to groups who are given authority and power to manage and regulate as they deem best everything in the interest of persons belonging to particular occupations and callings. That is the method that is adopted in Russia. It is part of the soviet system. But that method I submit is not needed in Canada at the present time, and is not necessary to effect regulation in the most effective way.
Again there are movements in other countries, as for example in Germany, Italy and Austria, where the effort has been made to get rid of parliament altogether and turn over the power to legislate to dictators on the assumption that parliaments in those countries have broken down and have not served the purposes and met the needs of the people.
I have nothing to say as to whether that is true of Italy and Germany and Austria, but I do sav that so far as Canada and Great Britain are concerned it is not true. The parliaments of Canada and of Great Britain still stand as the great guardians of liberty and security for all classes of people in ail parts of their respective countries. The exception that I am going to take to this particular legislation is that while it purports to be legislation to further the regulation of trade and the production and marketing of. goods, it is really legislation designed to do away very largely, if not almost entirely, as I think I shall be able to show, with the power of parliament and the right of parliament to control in these all-important matters.
In that' connection let me ask at once what are the principles underlying this legislation? As I have said, you have to look at the provisions, not the name of the statute to see what they are. In this bill they will be seen to explain why the government has found it necessary to divorce the carrying out of this legislation from parliamentary control altogether. When we examine the provisions of this bill we find that the principles are

My hon. friend all the time, even in his speech this afternoon, argues for the extension of state functions. How can you have an extension of state functions, let me ask him, without the creation of
{Mr. Mackenzie King.l
a bureaucracy? That is of the very essence of it. How can you possibly extend the functions of the state without creating a bureaucracy, and how can this bureaucracy carry out its functions except by the power of might, which is force, and which is always the power behind government and authority when it attempts to administer public affairs by a large extension of state functions? That is the answer I make to my hon. friend and to the members of his party. They have not come out and said: We are after force and bureaucracy. But the whole essence of the socialist state is founded on that, and my hon. friend knows it. No one knows it better than he does. He has read Cole's book on the method in which matters may have to be carried on for a time, he knows that Cole has said that the socialistic state will have to have a bureaucracy and be maintained by force, and that in the meantime as a step to that end socialists will probably have to allow Toryism to go very far to help create the needed bureaucracy and force and accustom the public mind to that kind of government. The members of the CC.F. to-day are congratulating the government on this legislation which it has introduced. Is it not a nice spectacle to see an hon member, the leader of the C.C.F., which party regards itself as the antithesis of Toryism, congratulating Tories on their legislation, as my hon, friend has done in his speeeh this afternoon and that because it goes the length of further extending state functions in a manner which will inevitably serve to create a bureaucracy. We have our Tory friends opposite introducing -legislation which, like the spider with the fly, is aimed at catching a few flies which happen to be at the far end of the chamber. They are prepared to walk into the spider's parlour for the time being to help the spider get through this particular legislation. But I am afraid the inevitable fate of the fly awaits them.
In order that it may be made perfectly clear, Mr. Speaker, that the principles of the measure are as I have described them to be, let me give a bird's eye picture of what is proposed in the bill. Let hon. members carefully consider what it is that we- are being asked to endorse. I might say, if one does not take the trouble to verify what one says by reference to the provisions themselves, the natural reaction to the picture would be that the measure could not mean anything of the kind, that it cannot possibly go so far. Let me give the picture.
First of all, in the regulation of trade and the marketing of our production in this country it might be asked, is it this parliament that is to regulate and say how much

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
is to be produced, or what restrictions there are to be on trade, or how sales are to be regulated, or is it some other body or bodies? The bill does not provide that this parliament shall do any of these things at all, but it does provide that they shall be done by some bodies other than this parliament and in part by bodies that are not in existence at the present time. That is the first statement I want to make. This legislation is to give power to bodies that do not now exist, to make regulations which will restrict production and restrict trade, and to create offences for which it affixes penalties -it puts in this particular statute the penalties that are to follow if what is set forth as regulations and orders to be made by these bodies that do not yet exist is not earned out. That is what it provides.
The first proposal is that a marketing board shall be appointed and that certain powers shall be given to that board. What are the powers? One power is that if a group of persons in any local district come together and wish to regulate trade as respects a particular commodity, or group of commodities, it may petition the government to have the production of and trade in that particular commodity or group of commodities regulated in the manner it suggests. The government is then to pass on the petition to this board. If, after looking it over, the board advises that it is desirable to carry out the scheme-I direct attention to the word "scheme"; it is a scheme, not a law that is to be carried out-then the governor in council-not this parliament; parliament does not appear again once this bill has been assented to by the representative of the sovereign-may approve the scheme and publish its approval in the Canada Gazette. The scheme then becomes law; everything set forth in the scheme as framed and fashioned in that manner becomes part of the law of the land to which it applies. It need not and probably will not, apply to the country as a whole. There may be one scheme in British Columbia, another in Quebec and another in Nova Scotia; there is no obligation of uniformity, it is simply a scheme which a particular group of producers in a particular part of the country have agreed upon. Once it is approved of by the board, it becomes law in that part of the country.
This provision is put in the bill to please our socialist friends of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. It was put there to catch the leader of that party just as he has been caught this afternoon when he said that this means the beginning of socialism. His objection was that the scheme was not large
enough, that it went just a certain distance, that it did not go far enough to suit him. It brought him, however, right into line with the government in supporting the measure because it is the beginning of the control of production and of trade not by parliament, but by groups which have united together to draw up schemes which are to be made applicable at their instance to the rest of society. Have we come to the time when that sort of thing is desirable? Are there to be no interests considered other than those of a particular group? Parliament stands for the necessity of seeing that all classes likely to be affected by legislation are heard from before legislation is imposed upon them. Does this law require that all classes shall be heard? It distinctly rules out all but one particular class and that the class whose selfinterest and that alone is to govern. Take any group, whether they be tobacco growers, apple growers, hog raisers or other producers. Let that group come together and let a representative number of its members petition that the affairs of their trade as far as production, sale and the rest of it is concerned are to be managed in such and such a way in accordance with some scheme they have devised, if the board, the minister and governor in council approve of that scheme, it then becomes law. What about the men who belong to other occupations and callings? What about consumers generally? What about the great body of labour that the hon. member champions so eloquently in this house? They may not happen to be the particular group that is legislating in its own self-interest, but they will all be affected by the law the group is creating. Not one of them is to be heard in advance of the making of the law. The fines and imprisonments that are to apply to anyone who dares to violate what becomes the law are put down in the bill but what the law is to be none save the self-interested parties are to have a word. As I say, this was all intended for Cooperative Commonwealth Federation consumption.
Let us see what is intended in reality. Even if there is no petition by any group, even if there is no request from any source, if the government of the day or an unnamed minister-the bill does not say what minister; it may be the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), or any other minister

thinks it desirable to restrict trade or to restrict production, then the governor in council may make such regulations as are necessary to
