restrict that trade or production or regulate its business in other ways. That is all to be done without any reference to parliament. Is my hon. friend willing to turn over to the Tory party of Canada the complete control of all trade, and of the direction which it is to take? That is pretty much what he is doing in the support he is giving this measure. I have heard him advocate the desirability of trade with all nations and all countries.
There are two blights, so far as policy is loncerned, which have been put upon the trade of this country since the present administration came into office. One is the blight of economic nationalism, which seeks to bring everything in the matter of manufacture and trade within the confines of our own country, and the other, which I consider to be worse, the blight of economic imperialism, which seeks so to direct matters by legislation, as for example the United Kingdom-Canada trade agreement, tariffs, national revenue rulings and the like, that whatever little trade there may be beyond our borders shall be confined as largely as possible within the British Empire with as little as possible relatively with any foreign country. There is to be found the real significance of the powers to be conferred upon the governor in council under this legislation. When the government believes it is in the interests of its own policies it may pass any order it pleases with regard to the trade of Canada, regardless of the legislation parliament itself has enacted or may enact.
Do hon. members realize that this bill gives to the governor in council the power to prohibit absolutely the importation of goods from another country which the government may allege it is in the public interest to prohibit? Do hon. members realize that it gives the government not only the power to prohibit imports, but the power to prohibit the export of goods from this country? That is the power given to the governor in council. This parliament is to part altogether with its right to say what is to be imported or exported; under the provisions of this bill, hereafter the governor in council will have that power. I ask: Since when has this parliament decided to throw up its hands in the matter of the control of the tariffs of the country? Tariffs will be of no effect after powers of this ivind are given to the governor in council. I have always understood that the great function of parliament was to control the revenues and expenditures of the country and that tariffs played a very important part both with respect to revenues and what as a consequence may be possible in the way of outlay. This legisla-

tion takes away from this parliament any possible control with respect to any article or series of articles coming within its comprehensive provisions in connection with which the government of the day may wish to prohibit exportation or importation. I submit that is going pretty far. As I have said, the effort is to get away from parliament altogether in the matter of restricting and prohibiting the importation and exportation of goods, as well as in the matter of regulating production.
The bill as it is presented to this house destroys all that we have been taught to cherish as the essence of British liberty. As it now stands, it destroys all that upon which our parliamentary system in the truest sense of the word rests. It is unconstitutional from beginning to end; it simply ignores the constitution of the country and the constitutional rights of parliament. I would go further and say that it is subversive of our judicial system, as I shall be able shortly to show. Men have been accustomed in this country to believe that they had some protection of their rights in property and the fruits of their own labour, in the judiciary of the country, that the courts of the land would have something to say as to whether or not they were to have their right to hold their own property respected and to do with it what they pleased. It will no longer be so, once this bill passes if it carries in its present form. This law declares that, once these different boards to be created in the manner I have described have made certain regulations, they may go to the extent of prohibiting a man from working on his own property or from selling his goods. That is to be the law, and he has no escape; all that the courts can now do is to see to the imposition of the fines and penalties here set forth.
We have had a good deal of discussion in this house about the unwisdom of the blank cheque, the principle of giving to the government or to anyone the power to dip into the public treasury for particular funds as needed, without control on the part of parliament, and we on this side have fought that proposal right along for four succeeding sessions. I believe that some of my hon. friends in the far corner for part of the time supported the Liberal party in that effort, but may I say that this bill repeats this very thing. It does not do so as an emergency measure to furnish relief, but it does propose to enable the government to do as it pleases with regard, not to increasing but to limiting production, not to expanding but to restricting trade. It goes a step further than that, for it takes the matter right out of the hands even of the

governor in council and allows a board that is not yet in existence, the personnel of which, so far, we know nothing about, to dip into the treasury, into the consolidated revenue fund of the country and take out moneys for its own purposes. In order to enable it to satisfy its own needs, are we in this parliament going to hand the public treasury over to some board about the personnel of which we at present know nothing, and shall know nothing even after this legislation passes, until the board is actually in existence?

Well, Mr. Speaker, upon what does our whole parliamentary life rest? It rests upon the control by parliament, the commons in particular, over the revenues of the country, over expenditures, over taxation. That is what parliamentary life rests upon and has rested upon since there has been a free parliament in any part of the British Empire. The essence of it is complete control over taxation by parliament itself.
_ What has my hon. friend been supporting in his speech? He was supporting this bill. What are our friendis opposite seeking in this legislation? The object of this legislation is to get away from parliament by the setting up of a board, the personnel of which we know nothing about, and can know nothing about until it comes into existence, and to give to that board and other boards powers which parliament alone should have. Let me read subsection 5 of section 3:
The board may, with the approval of the governor in council, employ such technical,. professional and other officers and employees as the board may deem necessary or desirable, and such persons shall receive such salaries or remuneration as may be fixed by the board with the approval of the governor in council.
There is no mention of parliament there- no mention whatever of parliament, and there is to be no appropriation by parliament of moneys for the purpose, the board itself on authorization by the governor in council may take what is necessary out of the consolidated revenue fund. The board is to fix salaries and the governor in council to approve. Let me quote subsection 6:
Ihe board shall be a body corporate and shall have power for the purposes of this act to acquire, hold and dispose of real and personal property.
Since I have been in this parliament, until the present administration came into office, the practice has been, when money was required for the purposes of bodies appointed under legislation, for an amount to appear in the estimates presented to this house setting forth the amount of money required, and for that amount or such portion of it as the house might be willing to grant to be ap-
propriated in accordance with the custom and practice of parliament for centuries past. That custom was abandoned under the relief measure. Now that, under the guise of an emergency, the government have succeeded for -three or four years in getting rid of parliamentary control in that way, we begin to see the reason that power has been sought all along. It is to give the governor in council, one individual,, a dictatorship. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) said that the difference between the executive in the United States and in Canada was that the executive there was one man while here it was a number of men. I told him that I thought I could point out that the executive here was still one man; it was the sovereign and in Canada his representative, and the Prime Minister admitted that. But it is the sovereign advised by the prime minister and his colleagues. To-day the Prime Minister and his colleagues have come to be the real executive, the principle however remains exactly the same; whether the executive is the sovereign acting in his own right, or the sovereign acting on the advice of his ministers, the responsibility ought to be to parliament; parliament should not be parting with its rights in order to turn them over to the executive. What does it matter if at one time the executive is a sovereign and at another a prime minister, supposing their powers to be the same and alike autocratic. We are face to face in Canada at this time with exactly the same situation-and I am going to refer to it a little later on-as the barons of Runny-mede were with King John. John, the sole executive of his day, asserted that he had the right to say what moneys w^ere to be spent and what was to go for this purpose and what for that. What has been suggested by the ministry opposite in this and other legislation? It is not that parliament shall have control of the money, but that the executive may do what it pleases with the public treasuiy with regard to those matters in connection with which it has been given and is now further seeking a free hand?

. The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act.
What is that other than a blank cheque? The government have already taken a blank cheque for use with respect to all their powers with regard to any thing that can be done under alleged peace, order and good government. They have a blank cheque with reference to all expenditures they may wish to

This is not an emergency. One cannot get away from the language of this provision: not parliament but-
The governor in council may from time to time authorize payment to the board, out of the consolidated revenue fund, of such sums of money as may be necessary for the purposes of this act.
That is as unconstitutional as anything can possibly be. It is setting at defiance the whole function and purpose of parliament, namely, the control of the expenditures of this country and the taxation. It is parting with that and giving it to an executive to do with as it may wish and thinks best. That is not the only such provision. Let me go a little further. Not only can they use the public funds in this way but-
The board-
This is not even the governor in council.
-shall, subject to the provisions of this act, have power-
What power?
-to compensate any person for loss sustained by exporting, storing or withholding from the market any product pursuant to any determination or order of the board.
That is, the board may go into the consolidated revenue fund and begin to compensate people. I have always thought that when compensation was needed, parliament was asked to vote the money necessary and an appropriation especially for the purpose was required.

To compensate any person in respect of any shipment made pursuant to any determination or order of the board to a country whose currency is depreciated, in relation to Canadian currency, for loss due to such depreciation.
I am not saying that there should not be compensation in certain cases, but what I do say is that whatever compensation is to be made out of public moneys, the House of Commons should say how much compensation is to be paid and appropriate what is necessary before anything is paid. To pay the operating and necessary expenses ot the board.

These are all evidences in this legislation of a violation of that most sacred of all principles: No taxation without representation, and control by the House of Commons over the expenditure of public moneys. Where is the public, as a whole, represented on the board that is to make expenditures in this way? The only real representation worthy of the name is that of this House of Commons which represents the whole of the nation.
I shall now come to some provisions that deal with the power to legislate generally. I have dealt specifically with expenditures of public money. The "blank cheque" is only one phase. Let me now cite wherein this legislation does away with the rights of parliament to legislate on other matters and turns this power over to other bodies. And so forth. Not parliament, but the governor in council and the board between them are to determine how far a law is to apply. It is to be remembered " an existing scheme " means the regulations made by a board and which have the force of law. Listen to this:

By parliament? No, by the governor in council.
Are my hon. friends opposite prepared to support that kind of legislation? Is anyone in this House of Commons prepared to support it, if he really understands it?- that a minister of the crown, unnamed, may if he thinks it desirable frame a scheme the purpose of which is to regulate production and marketing, and which, if he can get his colleagues to agree to it, then becomes part of the law of the land, and those who do not carry on their production or the sale of their commodities in the terms of what is laid down, not by parliament but by this scheme, are to be subject to fines and penalties and possibly imprisonment. If a minister of the crown will come with any plan or scheme which has anything to commend it, surely with such a majority as hon. gentlemen opposite have they could count on getting it through the House of Commons. If they cannot, they have no right to say that when this parliament is no longer in session or apart from this parliament, they shall be free to set up any kind of plan or scheme they please.
I pause to make clear what is meant by " a natural product." The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) assumed all through his speech that what is referred to is simply farm products. But that is not this bill at all. Let me tell him that this term has an application very much wider than merely to farm products. He pointed out that the British North America Act contains a clause which places agriculture under both provincial and federal jurisdiction, and argued that at least it would seem that under that clause something might be done. The products of agriculture are only one of the classes enumerated. Look at the definition of "natural product" as set forth in the bill:
(e) "natural product" means any product of agriculture or of the forest, sea. lake or ri\er, and any article of food' or drink wholly or

partly manufactured or derived from any such product.
That includes, to begin with, pretty much everything that it is possible to eat or drink, and also a great many other things. It includes boots, shoes, clothing, furniture and furnishings, household supplies and the like; it includes any article which can be partly manufactured or derived from the natural products mentioned. And you are giving power to this government to make a law with respect to who is to produce those commodities, how much is to be produced, who is to sell them, or whether they are even to be offered for sale. And, as I shall show a little later, you are making it a criminal offence if some man should by chance even offer for sale something that under one of these boards or schemes is prohibited or restricted.
Let us go a little further on that point. Listen to this:
12. (2) The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette-
Let me pause there-not by law of the parliament of Canada, not by any statute, but by order or regulation of the governor in council,-
(a)	provide that any natural product shall not be exported from Canada without a licence;
but also to quote first 12 (1):
The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette, restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product which enters Canada in competition with a regulated product, and the governor in council shall have power to make regulations to provide for the licensing by the minister of importers, or otherwise to enforce any order made hereunder.
Can we conceive of anything more sweeping? In other words, hereafter we are to be governed not by statutes but by such orders or regulations as the governor in council may make to restrict the importation into Canada of any natural product. What does it mean? If the government should make up its mind that it is desirable hereafter that trade shall flow only in certain channels, that it is not desirable for example that the people shall get oranges or coffee or sugar at a less cost by getting these and other necessaries from some particular country that would like to trade with Canada but that does not happen to be within the British Empire, then it may prohibit these goods coming from that country and say that we shall get that kind of product hereafter only from the particular countries within the British empire so designated or implied. This is economic imperialism which, as I said a moment ago, is
their pet policy. In the last campaign the policy was economic nationalism: Canada first, but it has since grown to economic imperialism: Empire first. This section gives this government power to say what goods are to come into the country and what may be exported out of the country. I do not think I need stress that much further. However let me re-read subsection 2:
The governor in council may, by order or regulation published in the Canada Gazette,-
(a)	provide that any natural product shall not be exported from Canada without a licence;
There you are! Now, Mr. Producer, no matter what you are producing, if it suits the governor in council-not if it suits the parliament of Canada, not if it is a law that has been put on the statutes while members of parliament from all parts of Canada were present-if it happens to suit the governor in council, whether parliament is in session or not, to say that you shall not export anything without a licence, then you will have to get a licence, and without it you cannot export. (b)	prescribe the forms of such licences, the terms and conditions thereof and the persons who shall have authority to issue the same;
That is a fine power to give to a government on the eve of a general election, to send around the country a lot of agents of the government of the day with power to issue licences to the producers in the different localities.

the governor in council may:

What freedom is there left to a producer? And this applies to all who have to do with the natural products named. Not merely those engaged in the various branches of agriculture but fishermen, producers of forest products and of all things that are manufactured or derived from the natural products mentioned are, as regards production and sale, all to be at the mercy of what the governor in council may do.
I know what the minister is going to say when he gets up to answer. He is going to say: Do you think we are going Act exercise these powers? We want them, Hu, we are

not going to exercise them. That is what we have been hearing all along. But when that argument has to be brought to the defence of a measure it is the strongest reason why the measure should not be enacted at all. We cannot afford to give to any government, as this measure does, power to do what it pleases with respect to production and trade.
Now let us go a little further. The governor in council and the boards to be established by him under this act may in the manner described create offences for breach of any regulations made. That is something new; that goes further than anything we have had up to the present time. Heretofore I have understood that parliament was the only body that had the right to create crimes and impose penalties, that the consent of the House of Commons and the Senate and the assent of the representative of the sovereign were necessary before any particular act could be made a crime. It is not apparently to be so hereafter. The governor in council may make any regulations he pleases and may prescribe penalties; any breach of such regulations will constitute a crime.	.
Now let us come to another point, which I wish particularly to stress. I refer to the right set out in Magna Charta that no man shall be dispossessed of his rights without the lawful judgment of his peers under the law of the land; not the law as made by the governor in council, not the law as made by some unnamed and as yet unexisting body, but the law of the land as known to everyone. It is an essential principle of liberty and freedom that the law of the land should be known, that it should be so known that every man as he runs may read. The law should not be something which is to make its appearance in the Canada Gazette after some board or governor in council, not parliament, has passed a regulation; it is something that should appear in the statutes of the country.

Mr. Speaker, before recess I was speaking of the principles underlying this measure and had pointed out that as one reads the provisions of the bill he discovers that its primary purpose is that of limiting production, restricting trade, and creating monopolies in the production and sale of natural products. I pointed out that the provisions of the bill justified the view that it aimed at taking from parliament and transferring to a board to be appointed under the statute, and to local boards to be appointed in sections of the different provinces, the power to make regulations with respect to the production and storing and sale of natural products, but that parliament itself is not to be the body that under the act will make whatever may be necessary in the way of regulations.
I had also pointed out that under this bill when enacted into law there will be transferred from parliament to other bodies the creation of offences, offences in the nature of crimes, offences punishable by fine and imprisonment, and that all that is expected of this parliament is to fix certain penalties without knowing what the offences are to which the penalties are to be attached. The penalties are set forth in the bill, but I do not hesitate to assert that not a member of parliament can indicate at the moment what the offences are to which they are to apply. They are offences still to be determined by local boards, to be appointed under the act or by the governor in council.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that legislation of this kind violates the fundamental principles of British liberty, violates our constitutional system of government, violates every tradition on which our parliamentary system rests. I cited from the bill numerous provisions, anticipating to that extent the discussion in committee, because as I stated I believed that apart from this evidence the house would find it difficult to conceive that principles such as this could be embodied in legislation introduced into this parliament by any government. I think I have given instances enough of the provisions to make clear the assertion that I have made.
There is a portion of the bill to which I have not yet made reference and on which I wish to make one or two brief comments, and that is the last part which provides for investigation into some of the matters we have been discussing. Let me say at once that I believe there are certain evils which investigation is much more effective in curing than is any penalty. Publicity is a means of letting the light into situations that will not bear the light of day, and may serve even more effectively than any .penalties that can be attached to the violations of the provisions of an act to avoid the evil which may be disclosed as the result of investigation. I welcome in the fullest degree any legislation which will pro>
vide for the fullest kind of investigation into industrial and commercial evils, but where there is to be investigation hereafter, care should be taken to see that innocent parties are afforded the same degree of security as that to which they are entitled in any inquiry which would be carried on in the way in
2344	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
which parliament has hitherto provided. This legislation with respect to investigation does away with the safeguards which ensure to innocent parties their rights and liberties. It creates an interference with industry, not at the instance of parliament, but at the caprice of a minister of the crown.
The investigations provided for are to take place by the minister on his own initiative if he so desires, or at the request of a board, and the minister's initiative in matters of the kind, however he may seek to deny that such is the case, is bound to be in a large measure the result of political pressure. There will always be open the possibility of believing that the investigation has taken place from a political motive, and that it is being directed towards political ends. That is bound to be the case where power is left entirely in the hands of one individual, and where the investigation is not provided for in accordance with some predetermined method which has been approved of by parliament as a whole.
The bill goes very far in regard to what it permits in the way of investigation. It enables the minister to name the investigators, to choose them out of a self-interested group, because it is the group that wishes to have its production regulated and has succeeded in getting certain regulations passed under the provisions of the act, and this group of investigators is given power to determine what condition exists that is against the public interest and that is detrimental in a number of directions which the act defines. They not only have the power to determine what exists in this way, but as a result of their investigation they determine in addition what the offence is.
The penalties, as I say, are set forth in the bill, and we are to be asked to enact those penalties into law. But the body that is to fix the penalties is not to be the body that is to determine the offence. While parliament is to fix the penalties, this bill asks us to hand over to unnamed individuals and unnamed organizations and groups the determining of the offences to which these penalties shall apply. I repeat. Mr. Speaker, that without actually reading the sections of the bill anyone not in this House of Commons and with the bill before him would say that this was a misrepresentation of the situation, that such could not possibly be the case. I therefore wish to refer very hurriedly to the sections which bear out what I have said.
Under the head of Investigations in part II I read:
In this part and in any regulation made hereunder, unless the context otherwise requires,
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
(a) "committee" means a committee appointed hereunder by the minister-
A committee of unnamed individuals and groups. Then it goes on to define what "spread" is. There is also a clause which deals with the power to authorize investigations:
16. (1) The minister may at the request of the board or upon his own initiative authorize an investigation into-
Look at the number of subjects:
-the cost of production, prices, spread, trade practices, methods of financing, management, policies, grading, transportation and other matters in relation to the production and marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion of any natural product.
As I pointed out this afternoon, "any natural product" means any product of agriculture, of the forest, of the sea, of the lake or of the river and any article of food or anything wholly or partly derived from any such product. This means that the minister on his own initiative may appoint a committee to inquire into almost anything at any time. This all is perfectly clear. What security is there for business when it cannot be carried on without undue interference on the part of the minister who may or may not exercise his authority for political reasons? What does this committee do? Section 17 reads:
(1)	Whenever as a result of any such investigation the minister shall have reason to believe that such a situation exists as requires further inquiry he may at the request of the board or on his own initiative-
It comes back again to the minister each time.
-appoint a committee to inquire into the spread in connection with the marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion of a regulated product.
Who are the committee? Subsection 2 reads:
(2)	A committee shall be composed of such number of representatives of producers and persons engaged in marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion, and consumers, as the minister shall decide, and there shall be a representative of the minister who shall act as chairman.
What are the powers of the committee? Section 18 reads:
(1) A committee shall have power to investigate all operations occurring in connection with or in the course of marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion of the regulated product for the purpose of ascertaining the spread received by any person in the course of such marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion, and whether the same is detrimental to or against the interest of the public in that it is excessive or results in undue enhancement of prices or otherwise restrains or injures trade or commerce in the regulated product.

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
In addition to having those powers, the committee has the determination of the result of the investigation. Section 19 reads:
A committee may after investigation as hereinbefore provided determine, in connection with any operation occurring in the course of marketing, adaptation for sale, processing or conversion of the regulated product, what spread is detrimental to or against the interest of the public in that it is excessive or results in undue enhancement of prices or otherwise restrains or injures trade or commerce in the regulated product.
That is not some body created according to the laws of the land such as a commission whose powers are definitely fixed by statute; it is simply a committee which has this power of determining what is detrimental, excessive and so forth. Section 20 reads:
A committee shall in the manner prescribed by regulations publish every determination made by it hereunder.
"Determination" is simply another word for "offence." The last clause, which describes the penalties, reads:
Every person who, to the detriment or against the interest of the public, charges, receives or attempts to receive any spread which is excessive or results in undue enhancement of prices or otherwise restrains or injures trade or commerce in the regulated produce, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars or to two years' imprisonment, or, if a corporation, to a penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars.
In other words, this parliament is being asked to give its sanction to possible fines to the extent of five thousand dollars and to possible imprisonments up to two years, in the case of individuals, without knowing the offences to which those penalities are to apply. Parliament is not to have a say in defining the offence; that is to be done by the committee which is to be appointed by the minister to make the investigation.
. I come back to the question of whether the fundamental rights and liberties of the subject are to be dealt with in that manner by a representative parliament, which above all else is elected to protect the liberty and rights and property of the individual. Under this act, if the bill becomes law, the committee is to create the offence, and the same should be said of the local boards which are appointed for the purpose of laying down the regulations, that is, the laws, the violation of which is prescribed as an offence. Are these to be representative bodies selected in the manner in which legislative bodies are selected or elected in Canada, in England, or any British country? Before hon. members of this house can have to do with the making of laws they have to comply with and have
others comply with certain laws framed definitely for the purpose of seeing that whoever may be concerned in the making of laws is duly representative of the people as a whole. The first of these laws is the franchise act. The only persons who have a right to vote in a dominion election are those who can qualify with respect to the franchise. No qualification of the kind is required for membership on this law making committee. Anyone whom the minister wishes to appoint may be appointed to the committee. Next, hon. members have to be representative of constituencies. The Representation Act ensures that all classes in alt communities shall have a say before any offence can be created. Nothing of the kind exists in this legislation. As a matter of fact, it specifically limits those who have to do with regulating and making the laws and regulations to the interested parties, to those who have to do with the particular commodities the production and distribution of which are being made into so many monopolies. As respects law making, it is not representation by population, but representation by occupation. In addition to the Representation Act, there is the Dominion Elections Act which has been framed to ensure that before any member of this legislative body can help to create an offence or to make a law, he must first be elected in accordance with the provision of a law that ensures a certain degree of protection to the electorate in the matter of its choice. But none of these particular precautions or anything like them are to apply to these boards which are to determine what regulations are to become law. There is simply to be a direction by the minister or the governor in council with regard to the new offences which will be created as a result of the investigation and determination of the boards of investigation.
One has only to ask oneself what will happen as a result of all this to see whence we are drifting. We may have one investigation in one province, another in another province and yet another in another. We may have one board determining one thing and another board determining another. But it does not matter what they determine, the penalty is the same for the man who has committed an offence, by not producing or selling his commodities in accordance with the determination of the board that makes the investigation. I repeat that one has only to make clear the purport of this measure as verified by its provisions to see how completely subversive of all that is sacred to British liberty
2346	COMMONS
Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
and to British parliamentary institutions and to British practice and procedure in matters of legislation the proposed measure is.
This afternoon the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation cited the Winnipeg Free Press as a paper that at times inclines his way in that it finds it necessary to say that there is much that is good in socialism. I do not think anyone who studies industrial problems will deny for one moment that there is not good in very much that is termed socialism. Neither will anyone venture to say that the socialist party is the one party having a monopoly of all that is good in the matter of social legislation. The socialist party have taken many of the aims and policies which belong to other and older parties and have claimed them as part of their own beliefs and convictions. That may be perfectly right and proper, but there is no monopoly in the matter of social legislation as between the different political parties. They may differ as to how they are to go about achieving their ends and what they intend to do when they attain to power, but as for any one party being the sole representative of social needs, and the one party whose policies alone will meet those needs, that, I think, is carrying things a little far. However, let us see what the Winnipeg Free Press has to say about this legislation. I am going to read a paragraph or two, and I shall do so for the benefit of my hon. friend in particular. When the legislation was first brought down the Winnipeg Free Press discussed it in an editorial entitled The Marketing Legislation. And here may I point out that the Winnipeg Free Press stands in a very signal position as a guardian of agricultural interests in the west. It is a journal in the city of Winnipeg, the interests of which city are more bound up with agriculture than I suppose are the interests of any other city in Canada, though of course to some extent it is true of all cities in Canada that their interests are bound up in large measure with the prosperity of agriculture. The hon. member saw the force, of that truth when he cited the Free Press. This is what that newspaper had to say editorially of the marketing legislation:
The legislation, from a cursory examination, appears to justify the estimate of it which conies from the capital. It is pointed out that nothing ever proposed, not even the War Measures Act, begins to approach it in the power which it gives to officials to regulate the trade of the country. It goes further, it is stated, than similar legislation in any country in the world having parliamentary government.
That was the first statement. What had that newspaper to say after a careful study
IMr. Mackenzie King.1
of the measure? In an editorial on April 3, under the heading The Dominion Marketing Bill, the following appeared:
The text of Mr. Bennett's farm mai-keting bill bears out Ottawa telegraph dispatches which said it placed immense and perhaps unexampled powers in the dominion government's hands. It is like no other bill in the history of the Canadian parliament. It confers on the cabinet at Ottawa, and' in some circumstances on one member thereof, authority to regulate, limit and even prohibit every kind of trade (domestic, export and import) in nearly every kind of natural product. This power is to be exercised by a national board and a number of "local boards," but these agencies will be created and controlled by the government. The bill, if it comes into force, puts an end to freedom of trade in all products (to quote its wording) "of agriculture, or of the forest, sea, lake or river," and in all foods and drinks partly or wholly made from such products, a category which includes such diverse commodities as ice cream and tinned salmon, beer and bread, sugar and beef. Sales of all these goods at home and in export markets, as well as imports of all of them, are brought under arbitrary and unlimited governmental control by this one statute. It is a bill rivalling, if not surpassing, the most notable efforts of the European dictators in the way of economic control.
That is a carefully and thoughtfully worded editorial which, I think, gives a just appreciation of this legislation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the leader of the C.C.F. party, speaking this afternoon, expressed the view that because some exception was being taken to the extension of powers on the part of governments in various directions, the Liberal party was holding to its old tradition of laissez-faire and did not want anything in the way of an extension of governmental powers. I think I made it perfectly clear to my hon. friend that the Liberal party, all. through its history both in the old country and in this dominion, has believed in regulation, but it has been regulation brought about at the instance of parliament. When my hon. friend talks about the Liberal party believing in laissez-faire what he really means to say is that the Liberal party believes and continues to believe in liberty. He is confusing the two. Now liberty and laissez-faire are not the same thing. Liberty is secured sometimes by regulation and sometimes by laissez-faire. Laissez-faire is simply a method, just as regulation is a method, a means to a particular end, that end being liberty, and when liberty has been threatened by too great an encroachment of officialdom or arbitrary power then the Liberal party has stood for liberty and for freedom secured through laissez-faire. When, on the other hand, the individual has not had sufficient protection, then similarly in the name of liberty and of freedom-at one

Marketing Act-Mr. Mackenzie King
time political freedom, at another time social freedom, at another time religious freedom, and, as at the present time, economic freedom -the Liberal party has stood for such regulation as was essential to that end. What we have stood for is liberty and freedom, secured by laissez-faire when that method was needed to get rid of unnecessary restrictions that bind and handicap and fetter the subject and deprive him of his liberty, also for liberty and freedom secured by regulation at the instance of parliament when to the acquisition and maintenance of liberty that method of securing liberty and freedom has been equally essential. I am sorry that my hon. friend opposite is interrupting me.

I hear some hon. members opposite laugh. I doubt whether some of them have heard of the Magna Charta. It is about time at all events they began to learn the most elementary lessons in government. To make clear to them the bearing of the Magna Charta on our present discussion I will quote from Green's Short History of the English People, the chapter entitled Under the Great Charter, 1215-17. Green says:
It is impossible to gaze without reverence on the earliest monument of English freedom which we can see with our own eyes and touch with our own hands, the great charter to which from age to age patriots have looked back as the basis of English liberty.
Please note that. I have under my hand as well a copy of Select Charters Illustrative of English Constitutional History, by Stubbs, a well known authority. This eminent writer, speaking of the great charter of liberty, states:
The whole of the constitutional history of England is a commentary on this charter; the illustration of which must be looked for in the documents that precede and follow.
That well expresses the significance and importance of this charter. Green terms it the basis of English liberty. Green continues:
But in itself the charter was no novelty, nor did it claim to establish any new constitutional principles. The charter of Henry the First formed the basis of the whole, and the additions to it are for the most part formal recognitions of the judicial and administrative changes introduced by Henry the Second. But the vague expressions of the older charter were now exchanged for precise and elaborate provisions. The bonds of unwritten custom which

It is in this way that the great charter marks the transition from the age of traditional rights, preserved in the nation's memory and officially declared by the Primate, to the age of written legislation, of parliaments and statutes, which was. soon to come.
I pointed out this afternoon that the legislation we are discussing is so vague that one does not know what it really means. As I indicated a moment ago we know what the penalties are, but we are not yet aware what the offence is to be to which those penalties are to be attached. That is a reversion to a condition that existed in a period prior to the Magna Charta itself. Green says further:
But all vagueness ceases when the charter passes on to deal with the rights of Englishmen at large, their right to justice, to security of person and property, to good government. "No freeman," ran the memorable article that lies at the base of our whole judicial system, "shall be seized or imprisoned, or dispossessed, or outlawed, or in any way brought to ruin: we will not go against any man nor send against him, save by legal judgment of his peers or by the law of the land."
Where is the law of the land to which at the present time those penalties are being attached? I ask that question, and I should like hon. gentlemen opposite to answer it. Nobody yet knows what the offences are to be; they are to be named, but not by parliament. The security to one's person and property is no longer to be in statutes and parliament and the law of the land, instead, citizens of Canada are to be subject to fine and imprisonment for what any board appointed by a minister may declare to be an offence.

and that we in this country, in common with all the countries of the world, were confronted with new and baffling problems? What has actually happened in the world-not only in this country but in almost every other? We find that the chief countries at least, Great Britain and those of Europe, and I think we can add nearly every other, have been so disturbed in their internal economy as well as in their trade relations with other countries that there have arisen all over the world new and startling methods of doing business. That is a simple statement of fact, yet the right hon. gentleman throughout the whole of his speech never paid one atom or one moment of attention to it. He gave no consideration to the difficulties with which the primary producer-agriculturists, timber producers, fishermen-have 'been confronted in the last two or three years. No attention was paid to their problems. There was not a syllable in his whole speech devoted to offering a solution or encouragement, or even recognition of the existence of these problems.
What on earth has Green's history or the opinion of the historian Green about Magna Charta got to do with the price of eggs or hogs or butter? If the right hon. gentleman would just watch the financial page of his paper from day to day he would notice that the agricultural population of this country, constituting as it does about half our population, have during the past few years been suffering under a price condition which made the carrying on of their business almost an impossibility. That has been recognized. Just what to do to change that condition is the problem.

Quite so; we recognize
it. Everyone who gives these matters serious thought recognizes it. It is easy to say: Raise prices and fix them. That sounds easy if you do not think about it at all. But when you address yourself to the task of attempting to raise, shall I say, the price of farm products or of other primary products to a level that will enable those who are producing them to live, you are confronted with one of the major economic problems of the time. The countries of Europe have been faced with the same thing to a certain degree, and I shall deal with them a little later. But I ask the right hon. gentleman, with regard to his reading us a lecture as he did for about half an hour on our disregard of the principles of Magna Charta, the Petition of Right, the parliamentary principles enunciated in thi reign of William and Mary, while we all value these old principles, what on earth have they to do with the problems now before parliament? What ought to be engaging the attention of parliament are the things with which we are now confronted, and in the brief time at my disposal I think I shall be able to show that there are some very real problems facing parliament.
While I do not for a moment suggest that this bill is a cure-all for the evils of the present time I do say that the Minister of Agriculture in introducing the bill offered to parliament a proposal worthy of its serious consideration. Not that the bill is perfect; not that its details cannot be improved; not that changes may not be hammered out on the anvil of committee discussions, modifying details here and there to meet the will of parliament. But the purpose, the general scheme, the theme that runs through the whole of this bill, is directed to trying to improve marketing conditions in this country.
I submit, further, that many of the citations of the right hon. gentleman as he proceeded with his discussion of the bill were not fairly made, because he would cite some portion of a clause and indicate that it was a violation of parliamentary rights, and suggest that it referred, for instance, to production when the clause does not refer to production at all but says that the producers of certain goods may get together. What for? For the purpose of the better marketing of their goods. That is the theme of the whole bill-marketing.

We admit, Mr. Speaker, that this bill is new and unusual in its character. But in this country, as in other countries, people have been struggling along under conditions that have been difficult, and have been clamouring for something out of the ordinary. Peoples all over the world have been very restive with governments because governments have been slow to depart from the beaten track. This bill is a departure; there is no question about that. But it is offered to the house in an effort on the part of the government to cope with unusual and difficult circumstances.
On the second reading of any bill it is supposed that the general principles will be discussed, but I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that nearly every speaker who has preceded me from the other side of the house has
Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens

discussed the details of the bill clause by clause, when there was no opportunity, under our practice, for the minister in charge to correct wrong impressions, to interpret the meaning of a clause, or to receive from the opposition and other members suggestions of improvements in any particular clause. I think the result has been complete confusion in the minds of members of the house as well of the public as to the intent of the bill. I submit it would have been infinitely better * if the details could have been left to be hammered out in the committee of the whole.
May I now turn my attention to the general theme, or, shall I say, the reasons behind the introduction of the bill. I shall be very brief in this portion of my remarks. Due to a fear in the hearts and minds of the people of Europe in particular as well as of other parts of the world there has developed, not during the last three or four years but during the last ten years, a tendency to erect barriers against foreign imports coming into their countries. This is based largely upon the desire of the people to produce enough foodstuffs to make them independent of other countries in case their fears are realized and another war should break out. I am not going into details; it is only necessary to remind the house of that fact in order that hon. members may appreciate the reasons why certain barriers have been erected against trade.
Another reason why the barriers have been erected is this: Countries have become bankrupt, bankrupt because of international debt, bankrupt because of their inability to meet their foreign Obligations. So we find that many countries erected

That is another reason. Exchange conditions due to fluctuating currency was still another. Some of the countries of Europe adopted the quota system, and this system has become one of the major methods of control of trade throughout the world. Nations imposed a certain restriction on the quantity of goods which might enter from a foreign country. I think I mentioned on a previous occasion that France, one of the most wealthy countries in the world, has some 1,300 items on her tariff under quota. These quotas are put on so that only a certain 
amount of goods may come in from other countries. Trade is allocated and directed and a monopoly created in their desire for the protection of their own trade. Greece does nearly all her foreign business by the quota system. She will allow only a certain quantity of this or that commodity to enter Greece according to the purchases by other countries of goods from her. All of this has changed completely the method of doing business.
The right hon. gentleman speaks of Canadian trade as though we were back in the days before the war or in the period since the war when these new methods were only in the process of development. He speaks as though there were no obstacles, no difficulties, no great changes or no new problems. If that were so there might be some grounds for the complaints the right hon. gentleman has made, but the fact is that there is not a country of major importance in the world that I know of that has not introduced high tariffs, quotas, inhibitions and other means of preventing the movement of trade. This is not because this government or his government which preceded it did anything to provoke such measures; it is because of conditions inherent in the countries themselves, chiefly the conditions which prevail in Europe.
I turn for a moment to some of the other reasons why this bill was necessary. I have mentioned the external causes, but there is an internal cause as well. Let us consider the change which has occurred in Canada during the last fifteen years. For instance, look at the development which has taken place in the creamery industry'. A few years ago there were hundreds-I was going to say thousands -of small creameries throughout the country. I could name half a dozen large creamery concerns which now control not the whole but substantially a large part of the butter moving to the markets of this country. This mass production of butter is internal to Canada. Take the packing industry. Within the last ten years quite a number of the small packing interests have passed out of existence and the control is now vested in two or three firms. This has created a change. Take cereal production: a vast change has occurred in the milling industry. In all of the realms of industry we find great organizations growing up for the handling of agricultural as well as other products. For the moment we are keeping our attention largely on agricultural products. This has brought about a need for a change in the marketing methods of the country. These products are now largely processed in the great centres and are marketed in large quantities, leaving the control not with the producer but with

Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens
the processing element which handles them. The bill now under consideration is designed to give some opportunity to the producers of agricultural and other products to get a fair chance in the markets instead of placing them under the control of the great marketing institutions which have grown up.
Unlike the right hon. gentleman, I am limited in my time, and I shall now turn to the bill itself. The bill has three major divisions. Before I state what those divisions are, let me say first that when the right hon. gentleman was closing his speech he referred to the fact that Canada was not like Great Britain. In that country there is one jurisdiction while in Canada we have a divided jurisdiction, that is, we have federal and provincial bodies. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) said this the other night and he said it in condemnation of the bill. Had he given the matter a little thought he would have seen that the very construction of the bill with which he differs and about which he complains was necessary because of the fact of divided jurisdiction. In the first part of the bill provision is made for the erection of a general board to exercise the powers inherent to it because of federal jurisdiction. That will be a very limited jurisdiction, confined to internal Canadian trade or the handling of goods within Canada. Of course, when it comes to importing or exporting, federal jurisdiction will be supreme. When you come to direct the marketing of farm products within Canada you find yourself confronted with provincial legislation. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni will recall that provincial governments have often found themselves confronted with a limitation of jurisdiction on their part which prevented them from carrying out certain schemes, such as that which the fruit growers of the Okanagan wished to put into operation, or that of the milk producers of the Fraser Valley. I am not saying whether these schemes were good or bad; the point I wish to make in referring to the two instances I have mentioned in my province-others might be mentioned elsewhere-is that an effort was made by the producers to erect an organization which in their opinion would give them a better chance in the marketing of their products in the great consuming markets. They failed because of a conflict of jurisdiction.
In introducing this bill the minister has divided it into certain parts. One part erects a board clothed with federal jurisdiction. Another part provides for the acceptance by the federal board of cooperation by provincial or local bodies. It need not be provincial-wide; it might be local. For instance,
a scheme, as it is termed, might be instituted in the Okanagan valley to deal with fruit. It might be developed, and it could come under the jurisdiction of the federal board, provided of course the provincial authorities gave the necessary sanction to that movement. It was for that reason that several of the provinces, knowing that this bill was coming forward, passed certain legislation, which might be termed enabling legislation to enable the local bodies or groups or the province as a whole to come under the jurisdiction of the federal board, or in other words to cooperate with that board. And so you have these two features.
A third feature in the bill, which might be referred to, and regarding which considerable complaint was indulged in by the right hon. gentleman this afternoon and evening, is the matter of investigation. In referring to this aspect of the measure I shall try not to violate the rules too far in going into detail, but I wish to discuss the question of principle and to reply to the complaint made by my right hon. friend this afternoon. He said that the committee provided for in part II of the bill for investigational purposes was in violation of the rights of parliament-that we were in a sense abrogating the rights and duties of parliament in this respect. I submit however that nothing of the kind can be read into this bill. The federal government having erected an organization that can cooperate with provincial bodies, surely there is no objection to such a body inquiring into spread, inquiring into the question whether or not the producer is getting a fair share of the consumer's dollar, to put it in a popular sense. That is one of the things we are trying to inquire into in the parliamentary committee. We all recognize that a parliamentary committee can never possibly cover the whole ground; we have had abundant illustration of that fact in the appeals that have been made to us to look into this, that and the other. But under federal jurisdiction, if parliament will accord this right and power, these investigations can be carried on. What difference on earth would there be between the work carried on by a body erected without all the formalities of a royal commission and the work carried on by a royal commission set up under the Inquiries Act? This government could to-morrow or at any other time erect a commission under the Inquiries Act to make an investigation into the very matters mentioned here, and it could be done at any time and parliament would not be consulted. Nor would there be any violation of the rights of parliament. All that this does is to recognize that in agricultural and natural products,
Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens

in the basic industries of the country, there is need for a very considerable degree of investigation; and, recognizing that, a committee is erected and made part of the act itself.

Take section 21, to which the right hon. gentleman referred:
Every person who, to the detriment or against the interest of the public, charges, receives or attempts to receive any spread which is excessive or results in undue enhancement of prices or otherwise restrains or injures trade or commerce in the regulated product, shall be guilty of an indictable offence and liable to a penalty not exceeding five thousand dollars or to two years' imprisonment, or, if a corporation, to a penalty not exceeding ten thousand dollars.
My right hon. friend objects to this because, he says, it removes control from parliament. But what does it do? It declares that any large corporation such as I have mentioned, or any body of that kind which indulges in a practice that is against the interests of the public, that is to say, charges, receives or attempts to receive any spread which is excessive, shall be charged with an indictable offence. Now what is an indictable offence? My hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) will I think agree with me when I say that the meaning of this is that the person charged shall be charged in the regular courts of the land with the offence in question. He is haled before the county court or the supreme court, charged with an indictable offence, and he has the protection of the courts of this country, as he would under similar circumstances in any other British country.
I appeal to the right hon. gentleman to be at least reasonable and fair in matters of this

kind. He charges us with a violation of the rights of parliament, a usurpation of the liberties of the people, and an abrogation of the right of the people to appeal on this, that and the other. But the fact is that all the rights of the person accused are preserved. All that this does is to declare that in connection with this class of business with which we are trying to deal, where it is found on investigation that certain interests are obstructing the fair marketing of goods by certain practices, then such people shall be guilty of an indictable offence and haled before the courts and dealt with accordingly. Is there anything wrong with that?

I shall explain that; in fact I was about to do so. I was about to say to the right hon. gentleman: What would he or any administration do under these circumstances? I shall not name countries, because I do not want it to go out that I am criticizing what countries in Europe and elsewhere are doing; but a certain European country notifies Canada that it has imposed a quota on, let us say, canned salmon. They say to Canada: Your quota of canned salmon is 150,000 or 750,000 or 500,000 cases, a certain limited quantity. How is the right hon. gentleman going to direct that? It happens that in this instance-and perhaps I was unhappy in my selection of it-that the industry kept within the quota without any difficulty. But suppose we had a huge surplus over and above that quota which had usually gone to that market; who is the one who is to determine whether company A or B or C or D shall have unlimited access and who is to be restricted? That is not a duty that we are choosing to bring on ourselves; it is a duty imposed upon us.
Let us turn, for instance, to something that is known generally-the question of live cattle going to Great Britain. I am not for a moment complaining about the action of Great Britain; that is their own business. But Great Britain has asked that a certain quota of cattle shall be observed. I think we shall probably manage that without any great difficulty, but if the point is reached where we must stop sending cattle over there, let us say for a few weeks, what authority will say which person's or company's cattle shall go forward? Who will determine that? Surely there must be some power or body to do that. I can name a whole lost of items where a similar situation may arise. It does not follow that that ends our market; it does not follow that we cannot ship more abroad, but it does follow that we are bound to respect the laws and wishes of the country in which those regulations are imposed and, moreover, they are and will be imposed whether we disregard them or not, so that in our own interest we must take suitable action so to direct our exports that the quota shall be observed.

In all these countries a quota system is in force definitely and absolutely and imposed against the other countries of the world. speechtext:
I shall tell him that the task has been a very difficult one. It has been part of my duty as Minister of Trade and Commerce in some instances through officials of my department to get in touch with exporters to ask them to try to adjust their business, and they have done so; but in the last two years these quotas have been extending rapidly, not against Canada only but against all other countries. The time has come when we must have in this dominion some machinery which will enable the government to regulate the movement of those goods if we are to keep faith nationally with other countries and at the same time to do justice to our exporters. If I cannot appeal to my right hon. friend, I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite who are interested in this matter: What other method would they suggest which we could use which would adequately deal with the situation?
The right hon. gentleman says: But oh, this bill will give power to a body-and I remember he said this with a sort of dramatic emphasis-not yet in existence. What is legislation brought before parliament for? It is for the creation of these bodies, and that is precisely what we are trying to do in this case to-night. We are offering to parliament a proposal to create a body to do these things. Of course that body is not yet in existence; it could not be. Why should my right hon. friend, with that facility of language for which he is so noted and that peculiar intonation, suggest to the mind of his hearers the suspicion that something is wrong? Nothing is wrong with the bill; it simply and boldly and clearly sets out what the government asks parliament to set up so that we may carry on the business of the country. Oh, he says, but

parliament will have no more control over the trade of the country; parliament is being asked to abrogate its rights. We are turning it over, he said, as did the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth), to a body not yet in existence. We are doing nothing of the kind. The very fact that this bill is before the house is a recognition of the rights of parliament. We come before parliament and tell of the difficulties with which we are confronted; we consult with parliament as to how those difficulties are to be met. In doing that we are bound to come with some definite proposal. Does the right hon. gentleman expect us to come to parliament and say: We are faced with a lot of difficulties and we do not know what to do; will parliament please tell us what to do? If we did that, the right hon. gentleman would very properly say that the government had better vacate office because it has no mind of its own. It is the duty of a government to formulate a scheme which in their judgment and in the light of their experience is one which will meet a given situation, and to present that scheme to parliament. This we have done. I repeat what I said in my opening remarks; I know that the Minister of Agriculture, in charge of this bill, will welcome in the committee all fair criticism and constructive suggestions from hon. gentlemen in any part of the house. I have no doubt that there will be suggestions that will improve the bill; if there are I certainly will join with him and with others in welcoming them.
Then the right hon. gentleman complains that this bill creates a scheme. He does not like the word "scheme," but I think it is the word used in the British act, so it cannot be very far astray. And he says that a group may be set up under the scheme, and he used these words, "all others will be excluded from that group, and some favoured group will have control." Now the right hon. gentleman knows better than that. What is the purpose of this part which provides for the erection of what is termed a scheme? As I said, we cannot exercise powers which are reserved to the provinces, and we recognize that there might be a group in a province or in a section of a province that wished to have a more regular or orderly marketing of their goods. Let me take as an example the apple industry, and in this connection I invite my hon. friend from Hants-Kings (Mr. Ilsley) to ponder what he said the other night. I think he made a most excellent speech; with much of what he said I find myself in accord. If I recall his position correctly he did not

Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens
object to any scheme or regulation that would control quality, but he did object to control of quantity. Let me point out a situation that may very well arise. The apple growers of Nova Scotia or Ontario or British Columbia, all more or less independent groups, could form their schemes, could come together under a federal board in order to market their goods in an orderly manner. I invite him to consider carefully what happened last autumn. Nova Scotia had a phenomenally fine apple crop, and other sections also had good or fair crops. All these crops reached proper marketing condition inside of a few months, I think from about the middle of September to the middle of November, and there was a tendency to pour the apples on the British market. Remember that Great Britain also produces very fine apples, particularly in the southern part; and these come on the market at the same time. Then, as I think he or one hon. gentleman opposite mentioned, Australia and New Zealand, whose apples are marketed I think in May, June and July, sent an unusually large quantity to the British market, so that the Australasian apples were still pressing on the British market when the British and Canadian apples came along. It happened that our apples were poured in there in unrestricted quantities with the result that the market was very seriously disturbed and in a measure destroyed. The Minister of Agriculture there was so much perturbed because of the substantial loss threatened to producers that there was a very urgent demand for the imposition of a quota and a restriction of imports. That restriction was not definitely imposed last autumn, but I do say that if such a condition arises again, as it may and probably will, I do not doubt at all that there will be a quota imposed. Would it not be much better if before such a situation arises the Canadian representative could go to the British Minister of Agriculture and discuss the matter with him, estimate the needs of the market, and then that we should allow our fruit to pass on to that market in an orderly way instead of crowding it on without regulation, disregarding the rights of the British producer and the conditions of the market? That is precisely the sort of thing we are trying to provide for in this bill.
My hon. friend was going to ask a question?

perfectly and would have been all that was needed. I suggested the other night how that could be brought about without the expense of the complicated and cumbrous machinery of this bill.

I agree with my hon.
friend that a substantial part of the trouble was due to the exportation of inferior grades. There again we see the necessity of this bill. But I do not fully agree that control of quality would be as effective as control of both quality and quantity. I have no hesitation in saying that either you are going to be faced with chaos in a number of branches of agriculture or you must have some machinery that will enable this country to direct its marketing in an orderly way.

began to take exception to a remark I made, and I think the words he took exception to were " all others will be excluded." But he did not go on to speak of that. I believe the minister misunderstood. His inference probably is that I meant all other producers of the same class of goods. I did not mean that. What I meant was, other classes in the community, persons belonging to other trades, callings and professions, and consumers.

I appreciate that point,
and the explanation. However, it does not alter this, and we will stick to the case I have given. Is it not desirable that the apple growers of these three provinces should be brought together in some common understanding of this export business? For instance our friends in Nova Scotia, who are only five or six days distant from the British market can pour their apples in while British Columbia and Ontario might be handicapped in that regard. Or British Columbia might have say 10,000 cases going through by way of the Panama canal in cold storage; the market is in danger of being flooded, and someone from eastern Canada pours his apples in and destroys it. No one, I am sure, desires that. Yet that is a condition that is very likely to arise. As a matter of fact the preference that we enjoy on apples, speaking of that particular commodity, will be frustrated and dissipated if we do not take great care in that regard.
I have already dealt with the complaint made by the right hon. gentleman as to creating a crime. I do not wish to detain the house further. There are a number of details that I should like to discuss, but I think it would be very much better if the various clauses of this bill were discussed
Marketing Act-Mr. Stevens

in committee of the whole, so that we may focus our attention upon the clause immediately before the committee and not deal with it in a general way together with other clauses without giving the minister in charge of the bill an opportunity to reply.
I will therefore conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker, with the observation that the bill as it is introduced is prompted by one desire only, and that is the desire to assist in directing the marketing of Canadian products in the Canadian and foreign markets. That is the genius of the bill; that is the object and desire of the bill. It may be that in order to achieve that end it will be desirable to, shall I say, have some measure of control over production if, for instance, there is a reckless production in some section of the country to the detriment of others in connection with our export business. Or let us look at it in this way: assuming that cattle are being exported that are not fit for the British market, is it not highly desirable that we should have some body to determine what cattle or what class of cattle should be exported? These are the sort of things and I could name a score of them-that might properly come under the direction of this board.
With regard to the manner in which the board is set up, I think it is set up as other boards have been created. It has been complained very bitterly that the salaries of those who are to constitute the board are not named in the bill. That is a question which might very well come up in committee. My hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) complained that the number of members composing the board has not been named, and I might indicate to him why it might be perhaps inadvisable to put that number in the bill. This central board, which we will say might consist of three, might find it desirable to set up committees to deal with apples, tobacco, hog products, milk, dairy products-

Yes, my hon. friend can carry it to other natural products such as fish and lumber. Assuming that this was desirable, would it not be much .better if the government had a certain amount of liberty to add extra members to the board if desired? That, I think, is the only reason the matter is left open. This is new legislation. This government will be back here next session; there is no doubt about that, and we will be back here for the next parliament as well. Next session, without doubt, we will be subjected

to close examination as to how this bill has been administered. There is no chance of parliament being deprived of its right to control and direct its affairs, but let me again remind the right hon. gentleman that in questions of trade, in questions that have to do with the processing, the marketing and the controlling of our natural products, in all existing statutes or in any statute that would be workable there must be a certain measure of administrative liberty left to the government or else the thing would be hopeless. Imagine having to come to parliament and ask for a resolution approving of the setting up of this, that or the other body. The right hon. leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Comox-AlSbcmi said the other night and to-day that in the British house they go to parliament and pass a resolution. The British house sits practically the year round. They adjourn for about a month at Christmas, as a rule; during the dog days in August when no one does any business at all they usually adjourn again, and outside of a short adjournment at Easter, the British parliament sits the year round. So they have a different situation; they are a small compact country with one parliament. Here we have the handicap-and I think it is a distinct handicap-of nine parliaments in the country in addition to our own. We have the task of trying to keep ourselves in contact and harmony with these various legislative bodies, at the same time carrying on the administration of the country, with this parliament adjourned for seven months of the year. Obviously it would be impossible to follow the British course and come to parliament in connection with the direction of an act of this kind. It would be absurd and ridiculous for any government to suggest that such a thing should be done.
So, Mr. Speaker, we offer this bill to the house, not as a finished product but as a new piece of legislation designed to meet an unusual condition which has grown up in recent years. We ask parliament to cooperate with us in hammering it into workable and suitable shape so that it may be administered in the interests of the country as a whole.
