Mr. Speaker, I am sure we were very glad indeed to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), in his fifty-five minute address, endeavour to give some reasons why parliament should accept this bill. His first remark was that conditions in this country were different because we are in the midst of a world crisis. When I heard

Marketing Act-Mr. Duff
him make that statement I was reminded of the words of Robert Burns:
0 wad some power the giftie gie us To see oursel's as ithers see us!
I remember reading in the newspapers the addresses made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce and other members of the government during the 1930 campaign; the world crisis was never mentioned. It was said to be purely a Canadian crisis; the world had nothing to do with conditions in Canada. Hon. gentlemen opposite tried to make the farmers believe they should have seventy cents a pound for butter, for one thing. The minister did not explain whether this bill is going to give the farmer more or less for his butter, but I think I can prove conclusively that whether it is a matter of butter, of wheat, of fish or of anything else, this bill, instead of * increasing prices will lower prices. The strange point about the minister's remarks with regard to the world crisis, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Rhodes) took twenty-five minutes to tell us that the world crisis had passed. Tonight the Minister of Trade and Commerce tries to tell this parliament that this bill is necessary because there is a world crisis in which Canada is involved.
The minister also said it was necessary to do something for agriculture. Well, it has taken hon. gentlemen opposite a long time to find that out. They have been in power for four years; for four years they have done practically nothing. Now the mountain has laboured and brought forth this mouse sponsored by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir). A strange thing happened, however, during the address made by the Minister of Agriculture when introducing this bill. During his whole speech he did not take one minute to tell us what remedies were proposed for agriculture or the other primary industries of this country. He spent a great deal of time telling us about a calf that was taken to the stockyards from somebody's farm and that lost weight during the journey, but he did not say a word as to what this bill would do for the farmer or how it would improve conditions in the farming communities or in any other productive industry. I remember also that in discussing both the resolution and the bill the minister did not want us to ask any questions; in fact he would not answer us when we asked him to tell us what the bill meant. These are the hon. gentlemen who now come here and tell us that this bill is going to deal with and solve all our troubles.
What else did the Minister of Trade and Commerce say about this legislation? He referred to the fact that Greece and other countries have restricted trade by means of quotas. Surely it is bad enough for foreign countries to impose quotas on goods exported from Canada, but the Minister of Trade and Commerce admitted that by this bill the government was not only going to help foreign countries put quotas against our exports but was going to say to these other countries. "We have put extra quotas on ourselves so that our goods cannot be exported to foreign markets."
What else did he say, Mr. Speaker? He said that there was no intention on the part of this government by this bill to abrogate the rights of parliament. I say, Mr. Speaker, and the leader of the opposition has said, that by this bill the rights of parliament are being abrogated. But that is not all. In addition to the rights of parliament being abrogated, the rights of the private citizens of this country, which in my opinion are as important, if not more important than the rights of parliament, are being abrogated by this bill.
In order to make an argument the Minister of Trade and Commerce referred to the apple industry, and he wanted us to put a quota upon it. It is quite evident that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is not very well informed so far as his department is concerned, because that is the department that has to do with trade and commerce whether internal or external. I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there is great objection to this bill, not only in the province of Nova Scotia where apples are grown and marketed, but also in the great province of Ontario; and I would not be surprised, although I do not know, if there was not the same objection in the province of British Columbia because only the other evening my hon. friend from Yale (Mr. Stirling) in his speech in this house damned the bill with faint praise. He did not come out flatfootedly in favour of it, but in his effort to support the government skated around the bill and said that perhaps it might be advantageous to the apple growers of the Okanagan valley and the rest of British Columbia. I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce or anybody else, who are the better judges as to how and when the apples should be shipped than the men who are growing the apples and the men who pay their good money to buy them from the producers of Nova Scotia, Ontario and British Columbia? Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce

Yes, and let me go further and say that when the Grits are in power certain interests and certain people will want jobs on that board just the same as when the Tories are in power. Does my hon. friend mean to tell me that the men who have put their money into this industry, the producers who ought to get every dollar they can out of it, are not in a better position to know when to ship their fruit than a local board comprised of heelers of one party or the other?
I go a step further. I say that this bill is not receiving the approbation of the people of this country. Those who have had a chance to study the bill are opposed to it. I say that the business men in this country are opposed to it and the producers who have had a chance to learn what the bill contains are opposed to it. I say further that within the next month when the people who do not know what is in this bill, but who naturally were hoping that there would be something good in it for the producer, when the common people of this country and the producers of agricultural products, of fish and of lumber, come to realize that instead of giving them higher prices this bill is going to drive the agriculturists off the farm, the fishermen off the sea and the lumbermen out of business by the restrictions it imposes, there will be general disapprobation throughout the country.
What does the Conservative press say of this bill? Surely if anybody should favour it we would expect the Conservative newspapers to do so. I have clippings here from four or five Conservative newspapers, but I have time to read only one. It is taken from the Montreal Gazette of March 27. Everybody will admit that the Montreal Gazette, even if it is a Conservative paper, is perhaps the sanest newspaper in Canada. What does it say about this abominable bill?
The provisions of the natural products marketing act open the door to more government interference in business and in a much wider field than any to which such interference has been restricted in the past. The legislation is evidently based upon the assumption that those who are engaged in the production and marketing of fishery, farm and forest products do not know their own business.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, suggesting that the men who go down to the sea in ships

and the men who work on the farms and in the lumber woods do not know their own business better than any Tom, Dick and Harry who will be appointed by the Minister of Agriculture?

I bow to your ruling that the
rule is very plain, Mr. Speaker. There is no question about it at all. If I am not to be allowed to read this article I will say that the Montreal Gazette, a strong Conservative paper, condemns this marketing bill in all its moods and tenses. It is absolutely opposed to the bill, and says that it will never be workable and that it is an interference with business in this country. That is sufficient for my purpose, when a paper like the Montreal Gazette condemns this bill in such a manner.
It is impossible for me in the short time at my disposal to deal with the bill at any great length. Consequently I shall deal only with one effect it will have on one natural product in this country, and I want to preface my remarks by saying this:	in my
opinion, instead of helping that industry this bill is going to drive it to the wall. Due to the policies of this government in the last four years that industry is practically on its last legs now, and it is going to be the last nail in the coffin, in my opinion, when this bill goes into effect. I refer to the great fishing industry in this country. I am going to deal with that industry in two of its phases: first, as to how this bill will affect the fresh fish industry, which is altogether an internal

Marketing Act-Mr. Duff
trade; and second, how it is going to affect the salt fish industry and the prepared fish industry, as far as foreign trade is concerned.
Let us see what will happen. Under this bill we are going to set up in this country different boards. What to do?
-to regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality;
What does that mean as far as the fish industry is concerned? In the first place; how are these boards going to operate in the maritime provinces, on the great lakes and on the Pacific ocean? Anybody who knows anything about the geography of this country and knows anything about its business, and surely the Minister of Trade and Commerce should know something about it if anybody does, knows that in the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, all along the Atlantic coast from Grand Manan to Cape North and extending up to Northumberland straits, there must be at least two hundred fishing hamlets each separate from the other. I want to impress that upon the house, that there must be two hundred different fishing hamlets from Grand Manan to Cape North. Will there be a local board set up in each community? If not, what good will a general board be if it is separated a hundred miles from the fishing community? Do you mean to tell me that the fishermen of Necum-Teuch will have to go to Halifax to consult the local board? Do you mean to tell me that the fishermen of Cole Harbour will have to go to Canso or somewhere else to consult the board? Do you mean to tell me that the fishermen of Glace Bay will have to go to North Sydney to consult the board? The thing is ridiculous on its face.
What is going to happen in the marketing of fresh fish? I claim that these boards will be no good and that they will not be able to carry out the functions which they are supposed to carry out as far as the fishing industry is concerned. What about the purchasing and selling of the product of the fresh fish industry? How can this bill help in any degree the producers of the fishing industry? The fishermen go out in the morning at four o'clock and bring in the fish fresh that evening. They must dispose of their fish immediately. We know what government officials or most of them are like; they interfere with every business instead of minding their own. These officials of the board will walk down on the wharf and they will say to the fisher-74726-150
men who have fresh fish in their boats: "You cannot accept that price of two, three or four cents per pound which the buyer is willing to pay you; you must keep your fish until tomorrow, the next day or the next week when it will be rotten so that the board can tell you when you can sell and at what price." That is what this legislation means. Let us assume that there is no interference and the buyer purchases the fish. He gets ready to box them up, he gets ready to ice them. Perhaps during the morning and before the fish were caught he had received telegrams from Montreal, Quebec, Winnipeg and other places offering him a certain price for fish and agreeing to take a certain quantity. This officious local board may be comprised of people who are the enemies of fishermen. They go down to the wharf and they say to the buyer: "You cannot sell your fish; you cannot ship them to Toronto, Montreal, Quebec or anywhere else." The buyer may have to show his telegrams and correspondence and the board may say, "You must hold this fish until to-morrow when the price will be higher. Telegraph your customer that instead of selling them for eight or nine cents delivered, you must have ten cents per pound." In the meantime the ice melts and the fish go bad. While the boards at Canso, Lunenburg, Yarmouth or elsewhere in Nova Scotia may be holding fish in that way, the boards in New Brunswick, whose officials may have more common sense, may permit fish to be sold. The result will be that the fishermen in New Brunswick are able to dispose of their fish while the fishermen in Nova Scotia cannot because of the interference of the board. That is exactly what is going to happen as far as the fresh fish industry is concerned.

My hon. friend behind me says that that will make a lot of work for the lawyers. What about the salt fish industry? I am again going to refer to my own province.

My hon. friend knows as well as I that there is a large salt fish business in Nova Scotia. The fishermen catch fish fresh and take them ashore. They sell them to buyers who split and salt them and put them down in puncheons. Provided there is no interference in this bill, the fishermen get their money when they land their fish. There are perhaps hundreds of people in Nova Scotia engaged in buying fresh fish from the fishermen and salting them and putting them in puncheons. For the sake of argument let us assume that there is no interference by the board as far as the purchasing of fish is concerned. The buyer buys the fish, salts them and puts them away in puncheons. He leaves them for two or three months. Perhaps he has used up all his owrn money and he goes to the bank and borrows money on the fish he is getting ready for shipment later on. He may receive an offer from Gloucester or Boston for this salt, pickled fish but the board steps in and says: "No, you cannot sell this fish in Boston or Gloucester at that price; you must wait for a higher price." Perhaps this man may be kept from shipping his fish for two or three months. In the meantime the market has gone down. Why? Because the Gloucester and Boston fish men, finding they cannot get salt fish in Nova Scotia, go to Newfoundland, to Norway if necessary, or perhaps to New Brunswick, where the board may have more common sense than the one in Nova Scotia. They obtain their supplies from those places. The result is that in three or four months' time, when the embargo is lifted and the local board allows the dealer to ship the fish to Boston, he has to take a cent or two cents less per pound. My hon. friend says that he is compensated; but, I ask, why should there be any necessity for compensation? Is it due to the stupidity of the officials appointed by the government? Is that the reason why the compensation clause appears here? Why does not this government allow trade to flow naturally? Why should the government say to any man, "You shall not ship your salt fish to Boston or to Gloucester even if you wish to "? That is the man's own business and the business of the bank that advances him the money.
This bill is not fair to anyone, whether it be the man who catches the fish, the man who handles it or the man who sells it. And what about our foreign trade? In the mari-times there is what is known as the salt fish industry. There is pickled fish, herring and mackerel, and my hon. friend from Cape Breton South knows that in the island of Cape Breton the fishermen catch tens of thousands of barrels of mackerel and herring.

Marketing Act-Mr. Duff
They go to the small business men in the community in the spring and obtain supplies -barrels, salt and nets with which to catch the fish. They go out and catch the fish and bring them in and split them or gib them, then they salt them and put them into barrels. Well, what will happen now? After the fish are ready for market this local board comes along and says to the fisherman, "You cannot sell your fish to the storekeeper in Louis-burg; you cannot even send them to Halifax until we give you permission to dispose of them." What happens? In other parts of Nova Scotia there may be thousands of barrels of mackerel awaiting shipment and the local boards in these other places may allow the fishermen to ship their product to Halifax or to other purchasers of mackerel and herring in the province, and in the meantime the Cape Breton fishermen are left with their fish on their hands. By and by the market goes down and when the purchaser in the West Indies has all his bookings made for five or six months-because that is what they do- and all his arrangements to buy mackerel and herring have been completed so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, when he cannot get the commodity in that province he will go to Newfoundland and the fishermen in Cape Breton will be left with the herring and mackerel on their hands because the board would not allow the fish to be shipped out.
And who is to determine the loss? The local board, the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Finance, who represents Richmond and West Cape Breton, where thousands of barrels of mackerel are caught every year? Who is to interfere, who is to fix the price, who is to use influence with the government to get the money paid as my hon. friend says the act provides? Who ever heard of business being carried on in this way?
Let me discuss something else in connection with salt fish. In addition to mackerel and herring, as my hon. friend knows, from Cape North to Grand Manan there are thousands of quintals of dried fish, cod, hake and pollock. This fish is caught and dried every year. Now, there is in the bill a section that provides that if the fisherman does not obey the mandate of the local board, if he does not take out a licence or do a hundred and one other things he shall be liable to fine and imprisonment. But what does the poor devil at Neil's harbour know about this legislation? He catches the fish and takes it ashore; he dries the fish and takes it to Halifax. When he gets to Halifax another officious local board appears on the wharf and says to him, "How much can you get for 74726-150J
that codfish?" He and the other fishermen with him say, "We have had four or five offers at such and such a price," but the board says, "You cannot sell the fish at that price; you have to get more money for it. You must wait for more money." The result is that the fishermen have to lie around Halifax until the board is ready to lift the embargo; otherwise they will be obliged to take the dried codfish back to Neil's harbour or to Ingonish as the case may be. If that happens, then next winter my good friend who represents the constituency in which these places are situated will come to Ottawa and inform the Minister of Agriculture that the fishermen have sustained a loss as a result of the order made by the local board, and the hon. gentleman will endeavour to get money for them-and none will work harder than my hon. friend from Cape Breton North-Victoria. But he will not succeed, and the result will be that the fishermen of Neil's harbour will have their catch left on their hands or will have to sell at a reduced price, because that is precisely what the effect of this legislation will be.
But supposing, after some delay, the fishermen are allowed to sell their fish to the exporter; what happens under this law? Let us see what it says, so that my hon. friend will realize that I am simply stating the facts. The board shall have power:
To regulate the time and place of marketing the regulated product, and to determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality or grade of the regulated product that shall be marketed by any person at any time, and to prohibit the marketing of any of the regulated product of any grade or quality . . . to compensate any person in respect of any shipment made pursuant to any determination or order of the board to a country whose currency is depreciated. . . .
Let me deal for a moment with that last provision. Why should the treasury of this country compensate me if I choose to sell fish in a certain market where the currency is depreciated? I will give an example. Two years ago, owing to certain conditions, the Canadian dollar was worth only 76 cents or, to put it another way, the American dollar was worth $4.24, while the English pound in Trinidad was worth only $3.80 instead of $4.86. Now, I was shipping fish to Puerto Rico and I sold my bills of exchange at a premium of 22 or 23 per cent, whereas in Trinidad I had to take $3.80 for the pound sterling. Surely it is a matter of trading. Why should this government insert in this bill a provision to the effect that if anyone sells in a country whose currency is depreciated the treasury of this dominion should compensate the shipper?
Marketing Act-Mr. Duff

Let us suppose that English currency were depreciated after the passage of this measure, as it was a year ago. It is true that goods shipped from Canada to Great Britain were paid for on the basis of 83.80 or $4.40, or whatever it was. But had it not been for the interference of this government, had they allowed the goods which the people of Canada bought in exchange for the goods they shipped to come in freely, it might have been as broad as it was long and no one would have suffered. But the trouble was that the Minister of National Revenue imposed a dumping duty to the extent of the difference in value between the pound sterling and a certain fixed amount.
As an exporter, I submit that this currency situation is all wrong, and the government has no right to compensate me if I sell in a foreign market in which the currency is depreciated. The Canadian product enters into competition with fish from other countries. Fish from Cape Breton and from my own constituency of Guvsborough, from Halifax county, from Lunenburg and Grand Manan, goes on the foreign market in competition with fish from Newfoundland, Norway and even Great Britain and the United States. It is a well known fact that large stocks of fish are put into storage in the fall of the year from October to December, and those stocks have to do until June of the following year. The exporter or the fish merchant buys those fish from the fishermen and he pays the fishermen the current value for them. If he has not sufficient money of his own, he goes to the bank and borrows it under section 88 of the Bank Act. The result is that in many cases large sums of money are loaned to the different exporters of fish in Nova Scotia. Those men fill their storage plants with fish; they pay the labour for putting them in; they pay fire insurance on the fish and they pay interest every month on the money borrowed. But when they want to sell some fish, when they want to dispose of the article, when they desire to pay the bank part or all of the money they have borrowed from it, this legislation steps in and some local board says: Oh, no, you cannot sell your fish in a foreign market unless you get a certain price for it. They compel the exporters in the first place-and I object to this-to expose to this board, which is not and will not be responsible to parliament, their private business. The result is that if this board so desire they can tell their friend who is in the same business as I am, what price I have been offered for my fish. They say: We will not let you sell your fish, and I lose the order. As I said a moment ago, the buyer in the
[Mr. Duff.l
West Indies-Jamaica, Haiti, Puerto Rico or elsewhere-if he cannot get the fish from Nova Scotia will go to Newfoundland or Norway for it.
Suppose the local board in Lunenburg will not allow me or another exporter to sell our fish. Perhaps the Halifax local board has more sense and will allow the exporters there to sell, and they will sell their fish and clear up their bank loans. The result is that I have a large stock of fish left on my hands in the spring. In view of those facts will the people of Nova Scotia, who risk large sums of money, be able to carry on business after this legislation comes into effect? No. What is perhaps worse is this: is there any bank in this country which will lend a man $50,000 or $100,000 to buy wheat, fish or anything else when it knows that under this legislation some local body may interfere and he cannot sell the goods on which the bank might have loaned the money? When this measure goes into force the banks will not allow people to do business in the way they have done it in the past and the banks will be fully justified in their attitude. My hon. friend says: All the man has to do is to say to the bank: Never mind, the government will recompense you for your loan if the merchant has to dispose of his stock at half price in the spring. If the fish turn red or dun and the merchant has to dump them on a foreign market, the hon. member for South Cape Breton says that the merchant can come to the government and get the difference. Who will decide what that difference is? I say that the thing is fundamentally wrong, and the Minister of Agriculture knows it is wrong because he is calling his friends together to-morrow morning at ten o'clock to decide whether they will withdraw the bill or what they will do with it.

speechtext:
I do know and my hon. friend should know, because he should be anxious to protect the interests of the people of Nova Scotia.
In my opening remarks I said that this bill would not benefit the producers of wheat, fish, lumber or anything else. In Nova Scotia at the present time we have voluntary cooperative societies which are composed of men in either the different farming or the different fishing sections. Those men in their organizations do good work; they get together, discuss their problems and decide what they shall do in their own best interests. But if this measure goes through, what happens?

Marketing Act-Mr. Duff
Every one of those voluntary cooperative societies goes out of business. Under this bill there is not cooperation, but a compulsory setting up of a local board of, say three men, not of fifty or sixty or seventy, as in the case of the cooperative societies, who to-day, all have a say. This measure compels the fishermen or the farmers to get together and so long as they have a majority of their number, the government will create a local board. Under this bill, if somebody has sufficient influence with the government, it is not necessary for the fishermen even to ask for this board to be appointed. So far as I am concerned, I have always been in favour of cooperative methods. In fact, in the town in which I live we had the first cooperative organization in the fishing industry or any other industry in the dominion. Sixty years ago this cooperative method was adopted so far as the fishermen in the county of Lunenburg are concerned. I have been in favour of that because I have been interested in the cooperative movement in that county for the last thirty years. But I say that this legislation is not cooperation at all; it is pure compulsion. Not only am I opposed to compulsion, but I say also that this compulsory method of appointing a board-and I repeat this-is not going to help the fishermen. In the final analysis the fishermen will suffer most.
The bill says that if a number of fishermen get together and a majority so decide, they can get a board. What about the minority? Let us say, for instance, in one of the villages on the Nova Scotia coast there are one hundred fishermen, and sixty of them sign a petition to the minister asking that a board be appointed. Because there is a majority the minister grants their request and appoints three local men to act on the board. The minute this board is appointed, what happens? They can regulate the time and the place of marketing and determine the manner of distribution and the quantity and quality of the regulated product. They can also prohibit marketing by any person at any time. Is that fair? Is that British? If sixty men get together and say: We want to hold on to our fish; we do not want to sell them, is it fair that if the other forty men want to sell theirs, they cannot do so, or even if one man out of the hundred wants to sell his, he is not allowed? He caught his fish; he and his two little boys went out at four o'clock in the morning in the fog and rain and storm and brought those fish to land. Yet because of this legislation, perhaps because some of his neighbours do not like him, they will prevent him from selling his fish. I believe that in
certain matters, for instance, in church and state, the majority should rule, and the hon member for Pictou (Mr. Cantley) will remember the vicious legislation passed by this parliament in 1924. We know what happened in that case. Not only did the minority have nothing to say, but they were blanketed in an organization under the bill. That is what will happen in this instance; the minority will have no rights. They will be told under this bill that they must sell their fish or wheat or whatever it may be because somebody else says so. Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask you to allow me to speak for a few more minutes, not very long.

Paternalism, or Liberty in Extremis
There were just ten commandments to govern us all
In the spring of our race, but now, in the fall, Their number is legion, we know not the half, To suppose we can keep all is surely 'to laugh.'
You mustn't buy tickets in lotteries bad,

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take much of the time of the house in discussing the measure now before us. I recognize that this bill contains very large powers. I recognize also that in order that a national board may be effective in carrying out the desired1 purposes it may be necessary for it to have very extensive powers. What I wish to say more particularly is that so far as the appointment of a national marketing board is concerned I am absolutely in sympathy with that proposal. As to the details of the bill, they can be left to the committee stage, when they can be properly discussed and amended where thought desirable by the house.
Unfortunately neither in his address in introducing the measure on first reading nor in moving the second reading did the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) take the opportunity to explain what in his judgment would be the scope or powers conferred upon this proposed marketing board. He did, however, speak of certain economic factors that must be dealt with and dealt with as soon as possible. Harking back to the ideas of twenty-five or thirty-five years ago is useless, for economic conditions have changed drastically since that time and we have facing us to-day a state of affairs such as the world has never known before; therefore extraordinary means must be taken now which would not have been taken then. So far, then, as the principle of the bill is concerned, namely the creation of a national marketing board to deal with the marketing of primary products, I am absolutely in sympathy with it, but I reserve my judgment as to the specific proposals embodied in the bill.
The hon. member who preceded me (Mr. Duff) dealt more or less exclusively with fish, something about which he knows. For the few minutes that I desire to take the time of the house I wish to deal with the industry of which I know something, in which I have been engaged in western Canada for thirty-two years, namely the agricultural industry. I think we all recognize that very few items of agricultural produce are selling to-day at prices which return to the producer the cost of production. I maintain that that condition cannot continue much longer, or the effect upon Canada as a whole will be very grave indeed. I am therefore willing to experiment to see if it is possible to assure to the primary producers at least the cost of production of commodities which this country requires and finds necessary to export in. order to pay for what is bought. If we go over the index figures for agricultural products, more particu-

larly up to about two months ago, we find that the prices, in other words the return that the producer receives for his labour, have been reduced to a greater extent than have the price levels of manufactured goods and other services. We are faced with this condition, that the majority of manufacturing processes to-day are controlled by great monopolies which can restrict at will the amount they produce, and to a very large extent tend to maintain their price levels. But each of the hundreds of thousands of producers of agricultural products in Canada is in competition with every other producer of like commodities when he comes to sell the product of his labour. The consequence is that so far as exchange values are concerned, the primary producer to-day is not getting a fair exchange. I am sure if this or any government can bring before this house a measure which will produce a greater parity of exchange values as between the different classes of commodities which the Canadian people must have in order to live, that will be all to the good not only of the primary producer but even of the manufacturing interests in this country.
The minister in moving the second reading of the bill told the house that he had received many communications from cooperative selling organizations. I think he referred more particularly to farmer organizations. He intimated that they were desirous of securing legislation of this character. I have not had the opportunity of securing much information as to whether the farmers of western Canada are satisfied with the proposals contained in this measure. I was very sorry, therefore, to hear that instead of sending this bill to the agriculture committee, where those who are most interested could come and give testimony as to whether the powers are sufficient or in their judgment too great or whether the general trend is satisfactory to their purposes, the minister proposes to submit this bill to a committee of the whole house. May I suggest to the minister that in my judgment, in order to satisfy public opinion and satisfy the producers themselves, it would have been far better to send it to the agriculture committee in order to give those directly interested, the actual producers of the commodities which will be to a large extent controlled by the proposed legislation, the opportunity of appearing and presenting their point of view. I suggest that that is absolutely essential. That is why I am not at the present time taking the opportunity to discuss the bill clause by clause and give my opinions

C.N.R.-Washout at Matapedia
on the various sections. But after all is said and done, sir, the most important thing in connection with any piece of legislation of this kind is its administration. It all depends on the administration of the legislation whether it will be successful and whether it will satisfy those whom it is intended to benefit. You might have the best piece of legislation the mind of man could conceive, but with poor administration the benefits would be absolutely lost. On the other hand you might have a piece of legislation considered poor, but with good administration it might be quite beneficial and effective. I would stress very strongly indeed that, in whatever form this measure passes the house, the government have a great responsibility in seeing to it that the administration is the best this country can secure, because unless there is proper administration I am satisfied that it will be a failure and will be detrimental to the best interests of the producer.
Let me repeat, sir, that with the principle of the national marketing of the primary products of this country I am in hearty sympathy. With regard to the provisions of the bill I want to hear a further explanation by the minister as to just how he proposes or expects to put it into effect, and until that explanation is given I am neither supporting nor criticizing this legislation. And may I suggest further that I trust the Minister of Agriculture will see his way clear to send the bill to the agriculture committee, which in my judgment would be much more satisfactory to the producer than to have the bill considered by the committee of the whole.
